integration towards a full banking, fiscal and economic union will require parallel steps towards a political union with reinforced democratic legitimacy and accountability. in a more fundamental sense, the debate about stability bonds and economic governance is about whether and how much deeper integration will be needed to reach these objectives. it is about the very nature of the european union, or at least, of the eurozone. finally, any progress or road map towards common issuance must obviously build on broad political acceptance and support from all participating governments and from civil society at large. therefore, much more work would need to be done to credibly and convincingly address the concerns of those governments and parts of the civil society that are currently not yet convinced of common debt issuance and its merits.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have the duty to thank the secretariat and all the shadow rapporteurs, because this was a meeting between decent people who have pursued the concept of the common good, avoiding ideological prejudices, and because we believe that the situation in the european union today is quite worrying. our economies are still in crisis and the downward spiral is still lurking. the crisis has had a disastrous economic impact, causing serious imbalances in national public finances, while widening divergences between member states. although gdp growth is expected to pick up this year, the short-term outlook remains precarious. the financial crisis is turning into a social crisis. just look at the unemployment figures: we're up to 11%. the situation calls for urgent measures: europe needs to grow again. the progress made in the new european economic governance is significant. the six-pack and the european semester have fostered a greater effort in fiscal consolidation, ensuring better macroeconomic conditions and a more stable financial situation. but that 's not enough . the process of adopting reforms must be accelerated: the two-pack is the case, as commissioner rehn pointed out earlier, also for other types of procedures, and we must achieve a banking union, which is a necessary reform for greater financial stability in the european union. other ways of managing and resolving the economic crisis should also be explored in order to minimise the impact on the real economy, although greater sustainability of public finances is undoubtedly the first step towards returning to growth. the consolidation of public budgets is a necessary condition for the improvement of the european economic situation. this consolidation must be done in such a way as to have the least possible impact on european citizens and businesses. the report therefore stresses the importance of consolidation based more on reducing expenditure than on increasing taxation. this reduction refers to all categories of unproductive expenditure, to all waste, especially that of the public administration, and to the inefficiencies of the various levels of government. the importance of maintaining all production costs, with investments in research, development and education, remains paramount. finally, effective action against tax evasion is needed, which is why consolidation must be implemented by cutting unproductive public spending rather than by raising taxes. this should be considered only marginally and only in the event that the cut in expenditure is not sufficient. up to now, raising taxes has been the easiest solution for some national governments, with the aim of reducing the amount of debt in the shortest possible time. but that only accelerated the recession. it is therefore necessary to review the measures taken to reduce the negative impact. however, consolidation alone is not enough: in addition to fiscal consolidation, national governments need to initiate structural reforms to foster a process of economic growth in line with the objectives we have set ourselves in the current europe 2020 growth strategy. the labour market must be improved by reducing taxation and the business environment to facilitate business activity, recovering the competitiveness lost in recent years and increasing the share of investment that can stimulate euro productivity. excessive austerity has displaced household consumption and slowed down firm output, marking a slowdown in internal market activity.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, let me again thank members for a very serious and substantive debate, which is in line with the seriousness of the subject we are discussing. the high level of public debt will be a key issue, if not the key issue, in the current decade. as i said in my introductory remarks as a comment on the report, public finances in the european union are gradually improving, and so, therefore, is market confidence in governments’ economic policies. the situation varies substantially across countries. this is why the commission applies a differentiated approach to consolidation, taking into account the respective challenges of each and every member state when determining the required fiscal adjustment effort. some members have referred to the question of fiscal multipliers in their speeches. i recall that hoang ngoc and several other members referred to this issue and to recent studies by the international monetary fund: the first one in october and a revised one in december by olivier blanchard, the chief economist, and daniel leigh. i want to say a few things about this quite briefly. first we agree with the imf that the fiscal multipliers are likely to be larger than usual when households are credit-constrained and monetary policy is already accommodated. we also agree, importantly, that fiscal multipliers vary across countries, across time and across economic contexts. from this standpoint, i want to particularly focus on three issues where the analyses and conclusions by the imf and the commission have converged, a fact that may have been lost in the controversy which has surrounded this issue in the debates involving economists and policy-makers. the first is that multipliers are as much about the growth effect of fiscal consolidation as that of fiscal stimulus. both the commission and the imf have found – although to a different extent, owing to the different country samples taken – that the most significant episode of understatement of the multipliers was for 2010, when most countries were implementing fiscal stimulus measures. there are good economic reasons why measures which are announced as temporary and are credible will have a more pronounced effect on growth. conversely, subsequent consolidation takes the form of permanent measures and the effect on growth is likely to be more subdued. second, multipliers are about the incremental effect of fiscal policy on growth. evidence that larger consolidations may have produced unanticipated growth shortfalls does not mean that reversing consolidation would have resulted in better growth outcomes. a lack of credible consolidation, particularly for countries at risk of losing market access, would have resulted in such a high rise in risk premiums as to offset or outweigh the benefits of a more lenient fiscal stance. in their most recent paper blanchard and leigh themselves very clearly cautioned against interpreting their findings as a call for reversing the course of fiscal policy followed since the crisis. i shall give you an example. think of italy in the autumn of 2011, say between september and december 2011. if italy, whose fiscal policy was already being questioned, had further relaxed its fiscal targets then it would have seen a very substantial rise in its already high interest rates, which would essentially have led to the end of sovereignty in italy. it really depends on the context, and varies across time, and we cannot have one general rule governing the conduct of fiscal policy in all circumstances. my final point is that there is empirical evidence, based on serious academic research, that public debt levels become a drag on growth if they get too high. debt levels in the euro area, especially in some euro area member states, are certainly too high. so the alternative of leaving debt at those elevated levels would also depress growth. we have to recall that public debt in the european union has risen from around 60% of gdp before the crisis five years ago to around 90% this year and next year. it is widely acknowledged that when public debt levels rise above 90% or 100%, they tend to have a negative impact on economic dynamism, which translates into low growth for many years. that is why consistent and carefully calibrated fiscal consolidation remains necessary in europe. i want to finish by saying that, in this context, there has been a lot of discussion about whether we should have nominal targets or focus on the structural effort. we apply a country-specific differentiated approach to fiscal consolidation, and each country’s consolidation effort is specified in so-called ‘structural terms’, which means focusing on the medium-term budgetary objective to reduce debt, and thus on the structural sustainability of public finances over the medium term. this implies removing the effects of the business cycle and one of the measures on the budget, and it means if growth deteriorates in an unexpected manner a country may be given extra time to correct its excessive deficit, provided it has delivered the agreed structural fiscal effort. such decisions were taken last year, 2012, for spain, portugal and greece. nevertheless, let us not forget that our level of public debt is very elevated. that is why we simply have to work with consistency towards the steady consolidation of our public finances and towards sustainable growth and job creation in europe.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank all the members who have contributed to the preparation of this report, the shadow rapporteurs and the members who have spoken today, because i think they are very interesting speeches. some colleagues have also made interesting comments on a whole series of proposed amendments, which were then accepted by compromise. but commissioner rehn is right: we cannot let our guard down, because the crisis is not over. the debate is still open and the criticisms of the use of the word 'medicine' for the disease are justified. let 's be careful . many times the drugs are worse than the disease, as you consider very superficially certain problems. i agree with commissioner rehn, and the report also agrees, that the question of budgetary consolidation is still open and of interest. the form it should take is still an open question there is no one who has the panacea and different schools of thought are emerging, both within the european institutions and in academia. there is a fair mix of taxation and public spending. i would like to make it clear in this connection - in writing. − mr. president, i voted for this resolution because i support the idea, launched by the commission, of having a council recommendation on youth guarantee schemes. this youth guarantee must be an instrument ensuring that all young eu citizens and legal residents up to the age of 25 years, and recent graduates under 30, receive a good-quality offer of employment, continued education or apprenticeship within four months of becoming unemployed or leaving formal education. the economic crisis has led to a rise in precarious forms of employment for young people and the youth unemployment rate has soared to 23.4 %, leaving 5.68 million young people without a job. in addition, all too often, short-term, part-time and unremunerated work is replacing existing jobs. recent studies have stressed that youth unemployment often leaves permanent scars, such as an increased risk of future unemployment and of permanent social exclusion. for all these reasons i am strongly in favour of the youth guarantee schemes.
in writing. - once again - the third time in a few months - the european parliament asks the member states' labour ministers to adopt a youth guarantee, following the example of some countries. this is a tool which provides that all young people under 25 and graduates under 30 who are unemployed - within 4 months of finishing their studies - will be offered a path to further studies, apprenticeship or work. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we are not under any illusion that this measure, if adopted, will solve the problem, but it is certainly a step in the right direction, to deal with a dramatic element of the economic crisis that is taking place. the figures for youth unemployment in my country have long since exceeded the alarm level, with an average of 37.1%. in other countries the picture is even more disturbing, affecting 50% of young people. finally, it must be borne in mind that any young person who does not enter the workforce risks social exclusion later in life.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on a youth guarantee because i believe it is essential to set up and implement youth guarantee schemes in all member states so that they receive a good quality job offer within a short period of time after leaving school. unfortunately, the youth unemployment rate has skyrocketed due to the crisis, and as a result, forms of precarious work have increased. in this respect, close cooperation between the social partners and employment services is necessary to ensure effective implementation of the youth guarantee programmes, through monitoring by the member states and by taking action where these guarantees are not implemented.
in writing. - i wanted to support this resolution, hoping above all that it would be a good omen and would serve to bring to the attention of all the very difficult situation young people are experiencing in europe today. the unemployment rate for this group of the population is rising steadily: in the european union, almost one in four young people are in this situation, and beyond the percentage figure, it is the number of individuals that should make us think. six million young people are in a difficult situation to find employment, with heavy costs both for the families who support them and for society as a whole, without taking into account that young people often feel frustrated and useless. this is very dangerous, because young people are the foundation on which the future is built and at the moment the prospects are not very rosy. it is not certain that a resolution will change the situation, but it must be a signal to governments to put young people at the centre of their policies and initiatives.
in writing. − youth unemployment in the eu reached an average of 23.7% in november 2012. in italy, the rate in the same month was 37.1%, while in countries such as greece and spain it is over 50%. with the youth guarantee scheme we are not trying to force job creation, but to put in place the tools that give young people a chance and avoid losing a generation. the aim of the scheme is to ensure that all eu citizens legally resident under the age of 25 and recent graduates under 30 are offered a good job, a new course of study or an apprenticeship within four months of becoming unemployed. i therefore urge the eu labour ministers to agree by february on a council recommendation to introduce this system in all member states.
in writing. - the problem of youth unemployment is now reaching the point of no return: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the youth guarantee scheme is designed to do just that: no young person in the eu should be without a job, education or training for more than four months. this is why all eu labour ministers must agree by february to introduce this system in all member states. the aim must not be to force the creation of new jobs, but to set in motion the instruments which give young people a chance to build a future by earning a present.
in writing. - i fully support this motion for a resolution, especially in the light of the economic crisis we are currently experiencing. in october 2012, the global unemployment rate had risen to an unprecedented 10.7%, with 25.91 million people looking for work. the youth unemployment rate has risen sharply to 23.4%, which translates into over 5 million unemployed young people, a figure that partly reflects imbalances between the supply of skills and the demand of the labour market, often regardless of the educational levels of those seeking employment. the member states are faced with a difficult and arduous task of stepping up their efforts to increase youth employment with the aim of ensuring that within a few months of leaving school, young people receive a valid offer of work, lifelong learning, apprenticeship or traineeship. the aim would therefore be to ensure that all young eu citizens up to the age of 25 and young graduates under the age of 30 receive a good quality offer of employment, further education or traineeship within four months of the start of the period of unemployment or the end of formal education.
in writing. − among the most dramatic effects of the crisis affecting western economies since 2008 is undoubtedly the dramatic increase in youth unemployment. in addition to the unemployed young people, many others are unfortunately employed in precarious forms of work, on short-term or part-time contracts, which all too often replace existing jobs. i therefore hope that the necessary increase in european funding for youth guarantee programmes will be achieved as soon as possible. i also hope that the member states will reform the rules on education and training for young people, so as to significantly increase the employment opportunities of young europeans.
mr president, the ambitious objective we set in the report on the role of cohesion policy in implementing the new european energy policy is the result of work done in the regi committee with itre and i must say that we set the ambitious objective that, after 2015, no region in the member states should remain isolated from the european gas and electricity networks. this fully reflects the significance of cohesion policies, also considering that the 2014-2020 seven-year period will probably be the few funds that will circulate in europe. that is why i have supported the dossier in this sense, so that there can be more effective and efficient spending. in this connection, i would draw attention to the situation in regions such as sardinia, for which several hundred million euros have been allocated to a project called galsi, which has been blocked for years by occult logic and represents a major international fraud to the detriment of europe, italy and the sardinians: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. it is clear that it is easy to connect sardinia and corsica with the italian mainland to the european network: instead, almost 1 billion euros remain locked in public coffers while unemployment at maximum levels and companies forced to go bankrupt are an insult to all of sardinia and the entire economy.
mr president, with the kolarska-bobińska report the regi committee is asking for a clear direction to be given to the use of the huge resources which the european union has made available for energy investments through the budget. the report sets out three main objectives to be pursued: diversification of the energy mix, improvement of energy production efficiency and the extension and modernisation of energy infrastructure. the second point raised in the kolarska-bobińska report is the need for energy policies to be managed in a less centralised way and to pay more attention to the specific features of the regions. the rapporteur's reference to the report published by the court of auditors at the end of the vote is of direct concern to me and i would like to say that i am certainly in favour of tightening the sanctions for those who, like italy, misuse resources, as is clear from the report; but i think we should also insist on more effective controls, clearer procedural rules and greater transparency of procedures.
in writing. - i believe that this report deserves support in many respects. the energy question is also vital if european industry is to overcome the present crisis. the achievement of diversification of supplies, security of supply and affordability for the end user are essential objectives; in addition, investments in efficient construction and transport would create jobs. i therefore voted in favour of the report.
in writing. − european cohesion policy aims to support europe's regions by bridging the gap between the most advanced and the least developed. in today's vote, parliament calls for the regional authorities, which are the closest to the citizen, to be the main partners of the commission and the member states when designing energy projects. these are very specific measures which must take account of the diversity of the territory: some regions need to focus more on the energy efficiency of buildings, others lack basic infrastructure in the distribution of gas and electricity, some are richer in renewable resources, others need to drastically reduce harmful emissions. it would be shortsighted and unrealistic to produce regulations that apply indiscriminately to very different areas. this is why cohesion policy must play a more central role in thinking about europe's energy future.
in writing. − eu cohesion policy can and must play an important role in defining and implementing the new european energy policy. as i have already said in the report, which i voted in favour of, cohesion policy can benefit from european energy projects. in line with the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy, territories can benefit from energy legislation that increases their autonomous capacity to manage these resources. while keeping the objectives of the two plans - cohesion policy on the one hand and the energy strategy on the other - separate, it is clear that the broad outline of european energy policy will be an important player in the recovery of europe's currently most disadvantaged territories.
in writing. - i have decided to vote in favour of the draft report on the role of eu cohesion policy and its actors in implementing the new european energy policy. the own-initiative report recognises the link between cohesion policy and energy policy and presents the following aspects: 1) european energy policy must ensure the security of energy resources, diversification of supplies and affordability for the end user. 2. sees european energy projects as a means of strengthening territorial cooperation and helping regions to manage their energy resources; 3. considers that investment in energy-efficient construction and transport is linked to the creation of new jobs; 4. recalls the importance of the structural and cohesion funds in achieving the europe 2020 objectives on energy efficiency; (5) considers that simplifying the procedures for accessing the funds is essential to ensure their efficient use.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report because i am convinced that cohesion policy can play a key role in exploiting the potential of innovation, research and development, so that future challenges in the energy sector can be transformed into an opportunity to boost the union's economic power. the common objectives of european energy policy are security of supply, sustainability and competitiveness. i welcome the overall approach of linking cohesion policy to the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy in order to embark on the path of smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. i also believe that initiatives to support local and regional energy saving capacities should be promoted, including through the promotion of erdf and esf investments.
mr president, this is not the first time that the european parliament has spoken in favour of eurobonds or stability bonds. so, maximum commitment by the community institutions to reform the mechanisms of the european union's functioning: this is primarily to get back to growth and job creation. above all, we cannot continue to have a euro zone that has a common currency but does not have a common bond market. this market would be necessary and useful not only for financial stability but also and above all for boosting development and investment. the commission has therefore set out a clear and credible roadmap for the introduction of stability bonds, accompanied by structural reforms to support growth and employment.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on the feasibility of introducing stability bonds, tabled by mr goulard, because i am firmly convinced that the european union must start to seriously consider the implementation of debt mutualisation and economic recovery instruments such as the redemption fund and eurobonds. the text as voted in the house represents a sufficiently acceptable compromise between those who want europe to concentrate its efforts on defining an effective strategy to support growth and economic recovery and those who maintain more rigid positions on economic policy. i certainly appreciate the many references to the importance of encouraging solidarity between member states, which is certainly linked to greater responsibility on the part of the member states, and the invitation to the commission to evaluate the possible scenarios. a common stock market is the logical continuation of the path taken with the introduction of the common currency. my vote in favour of the new wording is due to the need not to waste the opportunity for parliament to express itself clearly on these crucial issues, but i believe that the original text of the resolution, voted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs, would have represented a far more forceful alternative and a greater incentive for the commission to outline a more precise roadmap from the outset.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on the feasibility of introducing stability bonds because it is necessary for the european union to start seriously thinking about the implementation of debt mutualisation and economic recovery instruments such as the redemption fund and eurobonds. the text is a compromise between those who want europe to focus its efforts on defining an effective strategy to support growth and economic recovery through development and investment, and those who maintain more rigid positions on economic policy. it is therefore important to establish a clear and credible roadmap for the introduction of stability bonds and the implementation of a series of structural reforms in favour of growth and employment.
in writing. - i voted in favour of mrs goulard's proposal because i believe it aims to ensure a sustainable budgetary discipline which takes full account of the respective situations of the member states. the proposals concerning the use of certain instruments, such as the sovereign debt repayment fund, and the introduction of euro securities are interesting and useful. these two instruments, acting on two opposite but complementary fronts, serve on the one hand to guarantee the debt of the member states, in the perspective of an ever more cohesive and solidary european union; the commission has also proposed that the european investment bank (eib) should be able to support the development of the euro area by issuing securities which, given their characteristics, could be an attractive investment for a number of operators.
in writing. - it is necessary to urge the commission and the member states to explore all possible ways of introducing instruments for the mutualisation of public debt. this would, among other things, eliminate one of the most obvious contradictions in the eurozone, where there is a single currency but no common bond market. we must therefore act quickly and convince the commission to draw up a report on the various options for mutualising the public debt of the euro countries, drawing up a roadmap which clarifies the timing and modalities of its introduction.
in writing. − in the current economic climate, member states are having difficulty accessing finance at reasonable rates because of market distrust of public debt and the situation of european banks, as well as the ability of european leaders to take definitive action to protect and integrate the single currency. the crisis is demonstrating not only the interdependence between euro area member states but also the need for a stronger fiscal union with effective mechanisms to correct fiscal trends, macroeconomic imbalances, debt levels and budgetary ceilings of unsustainable member states. i welcome the proposal, considering that no federal state (nor the united states or germany) issues instruments similar to the eurobonds envisaged in options 1 and 2 of the green paper, and that they therefore fall within a completely new concept, not comparable to those of treasury bonds (usa) or bundesanleihen (germany), as instruments of proven reliability.

on behalf of the s&d group. – mr president, this resolution is the continuation of the long-term commitment of our parliament to the strengthening of the non-proliferation treaty and to its final goal, a world without nuclear weapons. a middle east weapons of mass destruction free zone, if it were achieved, would offer compelling strategic benefits to the region and to the world at large. the zone would resolve the iranian nuclear crisis and remove the danger of a ‘proliferation cascade’ that could include three or four additional middle eastern countries. the zone would eliminate the most dangerous weapons from the world’s most volatile region and reduce the risk of nuclear armaments being used in war or by accident. participation by israel and iran is critical to the conference’s success. iran has long expressed its support for a nuke-free middle east. on the other hand israel has much to gain from a verifiably implemented zone. its nuclear monopoly in the middle east is not sustainable over the long run, and a region with no weapons of mass destruction is preferable to one that has multiple nuclear-weapon states. the establishment of the zone would mean also the expansion of the global non-nuclear space through regional non-proliferation, which is one of the major achievements of the npt. the zone free of nuclear weapons now includes the entire southern hemisphere of the planet, plus large areas of the northern one. nearly 2 billion people in 120 countries live within the system of guarantees that reduces the chance of a nuclear armaments race and considerably strengthens the nuclear taboo. two entire continents, latin america and africa, are free from the most extreme threat to human security by virtue of the treaty of tlatelolco and the treaty pelindaba, which have been signed and respected by all countries. the same is true of the treaty of rarotonga, for the south pacific area, and the treaty of bangkok signed by the south-east asian nations. and a few years ago, through a landmark agreement which entered into force in 2009, all the five republics of central asia banished nuclear weapons from their territories. to the zones we have already mentioned, we should add antarctica, which was demilitarised in 1959, the sea-bed and the ocean floor, which were freed from the risk of becoming a repository for atomic bombs by the 1971 treaty, the territory of the moon and outer space. the outer space treaty, which was signed in 1967 and has been ratified by 130 countries, is a true renaissance manifesto of the possibilities of the human intellect. it not only prohibits any military use or territorial appropriation of space, but also establishes that every human undertaking outside the atmosphere should be carried out under the flag of peace and progress. why do we not extend this global pact to our continent, too?

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, for some 40 years the international community has been striving to create a zone free of weapons of mass destruction. the first proposal was made in 1974. the middle east is currently a zone of tensions and unresolved conflicts, and many states in the region have signed and acceded to international conventions and protocols on non-proliferation, including chemical and biological weapons, but in a substantially heterogeneous way. in addition, the international economic and financial crisis has aggravated the situation, causing controversial effects in the arms race: there are countries, especially western countries, many of them in the european union, which have adopted austerity measures in relation to their national defence and security budgets in order to stabilise their budget deficits. meanwhile, other countries, especially in north africa and the middle east, have increased their investment in arms considerably. the reasons are varied: they've increased them because of the controversial issue of iran's nuclear program. because there are revolts or real civil wars, such as in syria, but not only, egypt, bahrain, tunisia, yemen; the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force. so the 2013 conference is yet another opportunity to create a gun-free zone and to re-establish a climate of mutual trust and cooperation. we therefore hope that the high representative will do her utmost to ensure that the efforts made so far are not in vain.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when we discuss these matters, we always run the risk of missing the real objective we have to set ourselves. first of all, change our approach and our mindset towards africa and the poorest countries. what was once a concession, almost a favour granted by the powerful, the 'rich epulon', that is europe, to the poorer countries, has now become an agreement, a pact which makes it possible to improve conditions in that part of the world and at the same time to create the conditions for a reciprocal relationship, in which privileged access to european markets is now guaranteed for the poorer countries, and at the same time europe will also be able to gradually penetrate those markets. it is certainly a form of common growth between a great world power, the world's leading economic power, which is europe, and on the other hand some of the poorest countries in africa. on the other hand, as mr rinaldi has already said, in other parts of this part of the world, different attitudes cause far greater damage than we are doing with the clear improvement that we are bringing about with these interim partnership agreements. i would also like to stress, as mr lange has already mentioned, the protection of the rights contained in the cotonou agreements and the possibility that this agreement will pave the way for the accession of new countries to these agreements, which are therefore an extremely positive element in relations between the european union and africa at this time.
i believe that the important question of rules of origin is fundamental to the determination of the national origin of products. we know that the criteria used at international level are different: but i would not say - as mr fjellner has said - that when the rules work they do not change, because it is precisely this different interpretation at international level of the criteria that creates the objective difficulties that must be overcome. it is therefore becoming increasingly important that the wto members also achieve harmonization. at the wto level, negotiations are under way to harmonize rules of origin, the aim being precisely to achieve harmonization of the rules of origin and to avoid creating unnecessary obstacles to international trade. the criterion of the last substantial transformation is valid today: but the imco committee is in the process of reforming the customs code. in that committee an amendment was adopted on the basis of the principle that the criterion currently used has so far given good results at customs level and, according to that criterion, goods in whose production two or more countries have contributed are considered to originate in the country where they underwent the last substantial and economically justified processing carried out in an undertaking equipped for that purpose, which resulted in the manufacture of a new product and represented an important stage in the manufacturing process. the commission is considering the possibility of making the definition of 'last substantial transformation' more precise and more specific for certain sectors. we also suggested that the commission should be empowered, by means of delegated acts, to identify certain commodity sectors which may require a plurality of processing operations to identify the country of origin. it is a question which needs to be dealt with more fully and more fully, because today there are difficulties of interpretation and each country ends up applying within itself interpretations which are related to its own history and not to what is in the community's interest in the broad sense. we therefore support the european commission's efforts to harmonize these rules and at the same time call for strong action to be taken to clarify and reduce the number of disputes in this area.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission's intervention in the modernisation of the existing rules on the definition of origin is very important and necessary, and i think it would be wrong to underestimate the negative effects which have increased over time as a result of the different regulations which exist in the member states. the difficulties have increased: it's not true that the system as it is today works. then we must prevent the situation from getting worse. to do this, we must regulate the matter differently and i think it is very important to take account of the spirit in which, for example, the committee on the internal market has proposed a solution to extend the rule, with a number of clarifications. the last substantial transformation must be just that: it is not enough to change the buttons on a shirt to attribute the mark of origin to it. we must give substance and define with the greatest possible rigor and precision what we really mean by 'final substantial transformation'. otherwise, unfair competition will override the positive behaviour of the majority of our business partners.

in writing. regulating the non-preferential origin of goods entering the european union has always been a priority of this parliament, a priority never understood by the council, and one which affects our customs as much as the health and productivity of our citizens. we do not agree with the rigid set of rules which the commission has drawn up to ensure greater legal certainty in imports because these rules increase the confusion of our businesses and expose us to an unmanageable situation between different national laws for imports and exports to third countries. the legal certainty which the commission is trying to introduce is thus transformed into procedural uncertainty with the consequent increase in unfair competition and counterfeiting. in the report on the modernisation of customs, this parliament has already expressed itself in favour of the status quo for rules of origin while it has strongly called for a harmonized control system, which reduces the existing bureaucracy and at the same time monitors goods entering the internal market from any european customs. we therefore ask the commission to concentrate on customs harmonization and on a single regulation for the rules of origin for both exported and imported products.

member of the commission. − madam president, may i thank everyone who has taken part in this very lively debate so early in the morning. first of all, there have been a lot of questions about the wto. the rulings of the wto are quite clear. there are several by the wto appellate body that provide clarifications regarding the rules applicable to origin-marking schemes, and have led the commission to conclude that the 2005 proposal is outdated, in particular because it treated imported and domestic goods differently. for example, it proposed compulsory origin marking only for imported goods. in early october 2012, the commission reported on these clarifications to the council and to parliament. what does the wto appellate body say, in a nutshell? the wto appellate body showed that it was ready to examine origin-marking schemes in light of the provisions of the wto agreement on technical barriers to trade, something that was unclear beforehand. this could be interpreted as meaning that origin-marking schemes must comply among other things with the ‘most favoured nation’ clause and national treatment provisions of the technical barriers to trade agreement. in particular, products of foreign origin should be accorded no less favourable treatment than domestic products. the recent jurisprudence has therefore made more salient the issue of application to imported goods only as per the current proposal on the table. this would now be very difficult to justify in light of the interpretation of the national treatment provision of the technical barriers to trade agreements. some people have commented about the other countries. i do not accept that argument because what we are doing in the wto and also in all of our negotiations, be they bilateral or plurilateral, is putting a in writing. the european commission's decision to withdraw the proposal for a regulation on the indication of the country of origin of certain products imported from third countries risks undermining the guarantee of indication of origin and thus the traceability of products imported from third countries in the single market, at least for the sectors already covered by the regulation. the withdrawal of this proposal will have the greatest impact on european consumers and producers, who are already suffering heavily from the exponential increase in counterfeiting, which is destroying hundreds of thousands of jobs and affecting manufacturing industry without adequate means of combating it. i hope that the commission has planned further measures to make the regulation compatible with the wto requirements and that it intends to involve parliament in the subsequent stages.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union must have rules on 'made in'. the country of origin labelling of products imported into the union from third countries, such as clothing, shoes and jewellery, is firstly a necessary commercial measure to increase the competitiveness of european companies vis-à-vis their wto competitors and secondly a sacrosanct measure of transparency to protect consumers, aimed at enhancing both our quality production and compliance with the strict european social and environmental legislation. the obligation to mark the origin has been in place for years in countries such as the united states, china or brazil and, if adopted by the union, would simply put us on an equal footing with these other trading partners. with labelling that specifies the mark of origin, european citizens can be informed and know whether the products they buy are entirely made in non-european countries. the european parliament has already expressed itself on this issue in 2010 by a large majority and the commission cannot ignore this clear request by withdrawing the regulation just because no political agreement was reached in the council. we must redouble our efforts and try to find a solution to give the union clear rules on 'made in'.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there is no doubt that we are facing a huge problem, because i would like to recall that in october 2010 parliament voted by a very large majority - 525 votes to 49 - in favour of mandatory labelling for certain products from non-eu countries, such as clothing, footwear and jewellery. on the one hand, the defence of the consumer, who must be informed, but also the need for a europe which is fair to its citizens, which defends the rights of its citizens and of its companies. we are in competition with countries such as the usa, china and brazil, which have regulations on the labelling of products from other countries. can we then have the same rules as american citizens, brazilian citizens, chinese citizens or not? i think it is easier to have rules like theirs than to try to abolish them at home. i too, like jo leinen, expect the commission to come forward with a new proposal on this matter as soon as possible.
in writing. - mr president, parliament cannot tolerate the commission's decision to withdraw the proposal for a regulation on 'made in' and it cannot tolerate the behaviour of certain member states in the council. the 'made in' rules would allow third countries to sell their products in europe only by clearly indicating the country of origin on the label. first of all, reciprocity is a good rule: it is a paradox that these countries still have a choice whether or not to include this information on the label of goods sold in the eu, but at the same time demand (like china, the usa and brazil) that products imported from the eu bear an indication of origin. the european consumer is in fact prevented from distinguishing the origin of the products and making an informed choice. and our entrepreneurs face unfair competition every day. it is a totally failed trade policy.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution because i share the doubts about the legitimacy of the commission's decision to withdraw the proposal for a regulation on the import of goods from third countries, on which parliament has already expressed its opinion. the role of parliament in the decision-making process is thus greatly diminished, to the detriment both of the institution itself and of the citizens whom it represents democratically. the lack of a coherent and sufficiently strong organic legislation to protect the high quality of european products leaves our markets defenseless against the massive invasion of low-cost products from third countries. this is to the great detriment of both consumers, who can easily be deceived about the quality of the products they buy, and of european industry, which is subject to unfair and ruthless competition. we have a duty to move towards ever more effective control, and this regulation is an important step in that direction. to drop it is to give up this battle. i therefore believe that the commission should review its position and allow the legislative procedure to run its course until it reaches its natural conclusion, encouraging rather than preventing dialogue between the co-legislators.

in writing. - today we voted in the house on the report on 'the marking of origin on certain products imported from third countries'. the european parliament believes that the eu should make the use of the origin mark compulsory for goods imported from third countries. after criticising the commission's decision to withdraw the 'made in' regulation which had received strong support from parliament in 2010, we asked for a new proposal. as member states have not been able to agree on the mandatory indication of the country of origin for products imported into the eu, such as clothing, shoes and jewellery, the commission needs to explore other avenues to ensure a level playing field between eu businesses and their third country competitors and consumer protection. only a labelling of the country of origin of a product can ensure an informed choice by consumers and the commission is therefore asked to propose a new text to this effect.

the commission's vice-president - mr president, i should first like to thank the rapporteur, mr de backer, and the members who worked with him on this excellent report on access to finance for smes, which is the problem of problems if we are to win the challenge against the crisis. i also want to thank parliament for its support for the commission's initiatives and, in this regard, in particular, the action plan adopted in december 2011, but also for the support i hope to receive. we have already received some positive messages about this action plan for entrepreneurship which the european commission approved a few weeks ago. i agree with your analysis that the situation of small and mediumsized enterprises is still very difficult, even if the horizon has brightened somewhat in terms of financial stability. however, the economic situation remains precarious and smes are the first to suffer from these difficulties. we must urgently reduce financial instability and take measures to promote growth. we cannot always ask our fellow citizens to make sacrifices without having a strategy for growth. that is why the commission has been strongly committed to small and mediumsized enterprises, because only through them can we reduce the number of workers who lose their jobs. difficulties in accessing finance are common, but the problems and solutions are more specific. the reports emphasise the diversity of smes, more by type of enterprise than by country. it is this diversity that the commission has tried to cover with its action plan, which provides financial support, regulatory measures and political support. first, the financial support. the european union supports small and medium-sized enterprises through financial instruments for capital and debt, through programmes for competitiveness and innovation. in 2012, we were pleased to have been able to mobilise over €12 billion of guarantees for new investments and over €2.2 billion for venture capital by september. in total, more than 200 000 small and medium-sized enterprises have benefited from these measures. in addition, the european investment bank has almost doubled its lending to small and medium-sized enterprises, with €13 billion in financing in 2012 alone. i also want to mention the commission's proposal for a new generation of financial instruments, such as the new cosme programme, for the next financial period 2014-2020, which must be defended in this debate on the next financial perspective. the autonomy of cosme is very important, and i want to thank the european parliament tonight for its support. this is the first time we have a project devoted exclusively to the competitiveness of small and mediumsized enterprises. we have proposed €2.5 billion and a specific budgetary envelope of €2.4 billion for guarantees and access to capital. we also proposed that instruments be mobilised under the horizon 2020 programme, which is more focused on innovation. in this difficult budgetary context, we must defend the objective of growth and job creation, in particular through small and mediumsized enterprises. if we stop investing in our future, europe will not be able to return to the path of growth. the commission is working to speed up the implementation of the late payment directive in the area of access to finance. the deadline is 16 march 2013, but we have pushed member states to work before then. in fact, some countries have already implemented this directive. we must ensure that implementation in each member state is in accordance with the text in writing. the directive on the transparency of measures regulating the pricing of medicinal products for human use and their inclusion in public health insurance schemes is a very important directive which, in the light of recent developments in the field, has responded to the need to update the current regulatory framework which, although it has had a very positive impact, no longer meets the needs from which it was born. in this sense, the draft report under consideration, while fully respecting the exclusive competence of the member states in this field, aims to set out a framework capable of ensuring the application of transparent and appropriate rules to the measures adopted at national level in the field of price-setting and reimbursement, with the ultimate aim of facilitating access to more sustainable care for patients and at the same time encouraging research into new medicines. we hope that this approach will be maintained in all the next stages of the negotiations.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i went to thank the rapporteur because i thought her work was particularly effective and this underlines how important it is policy, madam president, ladies and gentlemen. the debate this evening is very important to all of us. fortunately, after years in which europe has focused on services and finance as the heart of the economy today, europe is beginning to discuss the importance of a modern, competitive and open industrial system capable of being a player in globalisation, to discuss growth which can create jobs and help us to overcome this great challenge against the crisis. this is why the european commission has begun, since the beginning of mr barroso's second term, in the framework of europe 2020, to stress the importance of industrial policy. there is no industrial policy as there was 20 or 30 years ago. it is a modern industrial policy, which aims to recover what we have lost over the last few years. unfortunately, today, the data on industrial production indicate a decline on an annual basis of about 2%, and the level of production remains below the pre-crisis peak of about 1%, at the beginning of 2008. the situation is, of course, different between member states and between sectors, but there is no doubt that the whole of european industry is suffering. that is why we must start thinking and working for change. as you know, i organized a great meeting a year ago in brussels on the theme of growth linked to industrial policy, where we invited jeremy rifkin to study a modern way of making industrial policy. there is a need for change, even if, among the member states, we can note the good performances of some countries of central and eastern europe, such as slovakia: up 18.7% on an annual basis, and lithuania: up 8.4%. however, other member states, such as cyprus, italy and spain, are in a much more difficult situation. even the largest european economy, germany, which had plastics. the situation is more simple for shipyards, chemicals and transport equipment. however, the problems are undeniable. i am thinking of the high-level working groups we have set up in the automobile sector, in the steel sector, and also in shipbuilding and shipbuilding. in terms of employment, after a rebound in 2011, the decline resumed, bringing the total of jobs lost in the manufacturing industry since the beginning of the crisis to more than three million, i.e. more than 10% of the total. the figures for the third quarter of 2012 indicate that there is an increase in job losses linked to restructurings. the 274 restructuring cases recorded in the third quarter resulted in the loss of 74 556 jobs. the sectors most affected were, as we have said, the automobile, steel and construction sectors. the crisis in european industry was linked first of all to the weak dynamics of domestic demand and also to the slowdown in international trade, which had been the main driver of the recovery. we must therefore act very quickly. with globalisation, industry has moved more and more to other parts of the world. over the last five years, china's share of global manufacturing production has increased by 7.7%. it now exceeds the united states and europe at 21.7%. in addition, our share in world trade in goods also fell from 17.3% to 16%. it is for these reasons that the commission presented in october an ambitious update of its industrial policy, as i said at the beginning of this speech, which sets a very clear goal: to reindustrialise europe by bringing the share of industry in gdp to 20% by 2020 compared to 15,6% today. of course, there is no simple figure, but a policy is needed to try to achieve this. the commission has therefore decided to concentrate its immediate efforts on six priority markets which can have an impact on both the emerging and traditional industrial sectors in europe. the six priority markets identified are clean production technologies, sustainable construction, bio-economy products, generic key technologies, clean vehicles and smart energy networks. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the programme to include the development of new technologies, such as the new generation of electricity, and to extend the scope of the programme to include the development of new technologies. the sectors which are or will be the subject of targeted action plans. i mentioned the car industry, for which the commission adopted the car 2020 action plan on 8 november last, which is intended to vice-president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all a political note. after many years, europe has returned to putting the real economy at the centre of its economic policy. after a few years in which all the attention was focused on finance and services, the arrival of the barroso commission 2 has changed the trend and the talk of industrial policy has returned. in 15 years of parliamentary activity, between 1994 and 2008, i did not participate in many debates on industrial policy in europe, on problems or on which industrial policy to have. i would say that there has always been little discussion of industrial policy at council level either. the time has also passed when the commissioner responsible - i remember the steel plan of commissioner davignon - had powers to make industrial policy. the powers granted to the european commission in the field of industrial policy are very limited, but there has been a strong political choice that has brought us back to focusing on the internal market, industry, enterprise, action to combat the crisis. if we have an economic policy based on finance alone, we circulate money and often that money ends up in the pockets of those who already have a lot of it. industrial policy, pro-business policy, creates new wealth and often allows for the redistribution of this wealth, using the market not as an end but as a tool for social policy. the change has come. it is not by chance and it was not easy, mr durant, to say and convince the whole european commission that there is a target to be achieved by 2020. the three "20" we have now are to be joined by a fourth, which is 20% of the gross domestic product, the result of industrial policy by 2020. it is a political choice of great importance and it is no coincidence that the council and parliament have also welcomed this political choice. it is not easy to move from policy to action, from the practical transformation of these choices, because a change in policy must have practical consequences which take time. i have not been oblivious to the arcelormittal case and to the steel crisis in general which affects my own country. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations. we set up the high-level group before the summer break in 2012, after a meeting with trade unionists from many european industries dependent on arcelormittal. we have set up this working party, which involves not only industry and trade unions but also the european parliament, as president pervenche berès and president sartori are also full-time members. the european parliament is fully associated with this high-level group which is taking time to find solutions. on the 12th we also involved commissioner andor on the employment side. i repeat, i do not have the powers of commissioner davignon who drew up a plan for the steel industry; i have powers commission. i can try to coordinate and find solutions to prevent clashes between different member countries. the same is happening in the car sector, not all the positions of the european car industry are homogeneous. the effort we are making is to prevent a clash between european businesses. then there is the problem of environmental policy. we are the flag bearers of the fight against climate change, but this choice also involves sacrifices. i have repeatedly said that we cannot, in the absence of a global agreement, go beyond the 20% threshold for reducing co2 emissions, because our industry is not able to exceed that target, even though it would be desirable. but we must be realistic if we are to prevent relocation which would also cause enormous damage to our action against climate change, because part of the industry would go to produce where there are no strong rules against climate change and this would also damage our action for the environment. as regards the concrete matters - because we have not only made general policy choices - we have included the steel sector among those sectors which are authorized to receive state aid, also as regards the quotas which can be reimbursed with state aid up to 80%. this was a choice which the unions themselves recognised as a worthy choice by the european commission. so something concrete has already been done before the action plan is put into practice, which takes time because agreements have to be reached and then approved by the whole college. it's not that we're not paying attention or not following. i am following very closely, together with commissioner almunia, who is responsible for competition policy, the development of the tyssenkrupp affair, the sale - as vice-president angelilli is well aware - of a major part of it to a finnish company. we have many community rules, not only industrial policy, but also environmental policy and competition policy, which often require us to make choices which can then have repercussions, in particular, which require subsequent action. i believe that the commission is also doing a good job in protecting our companies. it is no coincidence that there has been a seminar devoted to the competitiveness of our industrial system, as president barroso wanted. it is not by chance that trade policy is also being looked at carefully because it is not a naive trade policy. anti-dumping measures were adopted to prevent unfair competition. i am a firm believer in the need for a level playing field, competition must be global but the same rules must be followed. we cannot play the same football match in brussels 11 against 11 and then go to beijing to play 9 against 13, because that would be a lost match. we have raised many problems, including the problem of protecting our know-how, which does not mean being protectionist or closing the doors to our market, but looking carefully at the defence of our capabilities. we are also working hard on the quality and competitiveness of our enterprises in the field of key enabling technologies. on the 12th, there will be a meeting with ministers from a number of countries in the centre of grenoble which is one of the most competitive in terms of enabling key technologies. the choice of horizon 2020 is also a choice that involves change: for the first time, research will no longer be an end in itself, but will be directed towards industrial policy, because we can no longer afford to have chinese or japanese industries legitimately use our research results to compete against our companies, because there is no strong link between universities, research and industry. these are mistakes which we must not make again, mistakes which are the result of a reality in which industrial policy was unfortunately pushed into the corner, and was considered to be secondary. now he's not. the commission's choice has always been very clear, and the policy for reindustrialisation is the result of a document, at the beginning of this commission, which dealt with industrial policy. we are working very hard on the internationalisation of companies against the relocation. i have accompanied dozens of european industries in south america, north africa and the united states of america to conduct industrial policy on growth and a modern, competitive and environmentally friendly industrial policy. we called jeremy rifkin to discuss with us this third industrial revolution. the change has been made, but it takes time and there has been no shortage of concrete action, and i believe there will be. the final work of the cars21 high-level group has also led to the creation of a working group which will give birth to another action plan for the car industry, on which we are already working, which is a sector that suffers as much as the steel industry but is also the steel industry's main customer. we are doing a lot with results that even the most skeptical among entrepreneurs have acknowledged to the european commission. we are doing the same for the shipbuilding sectors by involving the european investment bank. we are making enormous efforts to give europe back its modern industrial policy. we must transform the council into the council for industrial competitiveness in certain sessions. we cannot discuss industrial policy with only the number two or three of the important representatives of the different member states. when it comes to making political choices, it is necessary for ministers to be present and to discuss. that is why, on 9 december, i convened for the first time informally all the ministers of industry to discuss the car crisis and the crisis in the main sectors, to the satisfaction of all the ministers who believe in strong action by the european union. the letter i received a few months ago from seven eu industry ministers asking the european commission for strong coordination action was a message i took up and turned into concrete action. i repeat for the umpteenth time that the powers we have are what they are, they are those which are entrusted to us by the treaty, they are not those which commissioner davignon had when he was able to put forward - he said so himself - a plan for the steel industry. if i had the powers, i would certainly have made a proposal in that direction, but i do not have the powers to do so and i have to respect the treaties. i would like to reassure all the members who have taken part in this debate. it is good that there has been another industrial policy debate, it is an indication of change. we continue to discuss ideas and proposals on how we want to have a modern industrial policy which respects the environment and which is in fact geared towards a green economy, which creates jobs. we cannot think of buying quantity with india, china, russia, the united states, the emerging countries of south america, but we can compete on quality and i believe that we still have a lot of cards to win this challenge. we think of the space industry and all the benefits that will come from the work of galileo, our satellite project which will be operational by the end of 2014. the uk government itself, together with the european commission, organised a major event dedicated to the services and service companies that will apply galileo signals on the ground in the fields of agriculture, fisheries, transport and health, for the protection of the environment and the fight against climate change. so this is the new industrial model. the british government, which often expresses reservations about certain community policy choices, is also a leading player in this new, modern industrial policy, and is one of the leading states with us. so we have to move forward, we have to have the courage and the strength to continue on the path we have marked, which is to continue to reinforce the change. it is certainly my task to do everything possible, but i need the support of the european parliament to be able to make this breakthrough that president barroso has wanted with the guidance of the commission. the choices have been made very clearly. we must now move forward, we must have the courage to face the problems with the powers that have been given to us and convince all the member states that a modern industrial policy is the best instrument to overcome the crisis that has been gripping europe for years. i'm absolutely sure of it. madam president, i apologize for the length of my remarks, but i think that a subject like this deserves to be dealt with within the limited time allowed us to respond to the comments made by the honourable members during the debate. i believe that the issue of industrial policy is one of the key issues of our economic policy and so i thank all of you for your contribution, including your strong and harsh criticism which i believe shows how much desire there is, how much enthusiasm there is in the heart of each one of us to work for the economic growth of our european union. i thank you for this and confirm my total commitment to ensuring that europe can once again become a modern, competitive industrial reality, certainly different from the industrial europe of the 1980s but certainly at the forefront, especially in terms of quality.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i would first like to thank the shadow rapporteurs and the opinion rapporteurs for their valuable contribution to the report. for a long time we have been confronted with two opposing interpretations of social responsibility: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens and mutagens is a very good one. as is often the case, i believe that the truth lies somewhere in the middle. i therefore agree with the commission's new definition, which neutralizes the opposition between voluntary and mandatory approaches which had so far polarized the discussions. the plurality of regulatory approaches shows that social responsibility develops on the basis of various processes which include both voluntary and binding elements. on the basis of these considerations, i have identified three areas of intervention for the future development of social responsibility. first, the link between social responsibility and competitiveness will need to be strengthened. it is becoming increasingly clear, more and more obvious, that social responsibility contributes to increasing the competitiveness of a company. this does not mean that any form of social responsibility reinforces the competitive advantage of the company, but that certain actions can enhance a company if they create shared value between the company, its stakeholders and society in general. in other words, whether these actions make it possible to strengthen the reciprocity between the commercial strategies of enterprises and the social context in which they operate. for this reason, it is necessary to encourage innovative business solutions, such as intelligent transport or eco-efficient products, which enable businesses to address social and environmental challenges while strengthening their market position. a second area of intervention concerns the broader objective of improving the transparency and effectiveness of social responsibility policies. this is a commitment that goes hand in hand with efforts to increase the level of public confidence. i therefore agree with the objectives of improving the processes of self-regulation and co-regulation of undertakings. finally, as regards the possibility of regulating the transparency of social and environmental information, it is essential that any intervention in this respect be compatible with the multidimensional nature of social responsibility and grant enterprises the necessary operational flexibility without causing additional administrative burdens. finally, the third aspect concerns the relationship between social responsibility and small and mediumsized enterprises. smes can not only facilitate the spread of social responsibility, but they have the potential to tackle social and environmental problems collectively, reducing costs and multiplying benefits. public authorities should therefore promote the dissemination of social responsibility among smes by, for example, supporting the role of intermediary organisations. similarly, guides or manuals or even specific strategies could be developed, especially for micro-enterprises. in short, the relationship between smes and social responsibility is a relatively unexplored area of action which deserves specific consideration, taking into account the specific characteristics of smes and their intuitive approach to social responsibility. i would like to end by reiterating to vice-president tajani the support of this parliament for the strategy and the firm will to follow it closely and to contribute actively together.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, if the house votes tomorrow on the texts of the two reports we are discussing, this parliament will have taken the most significant step forward on the subject of social responsibility since jacques delors, exactly 20 years ago, in his white paper, first identified this sum of measures as being necessary to give quality and prospects to the european production system. i think that the new features which are contained in it and which have already been largely indicated are important, starting with the one concerning the abolition of voluntary membership. the issue is no longer about ensuring that businesses recover or build a reputation, but about using these policies to have a positive relationship with the community and its joints, a community in which businesses operate. then the merit elements that have been introduced have their value as well. the definition of corporate governance as an element of social responsibility assessment, as not all organisations give explicit signals of responsibility. the detection of anomalies: the use of individual bonuses for the remuneration of employees or managers, especially in crisis situations, is not responsible behaviour on the part of any undertaking. respect, loyalty in tax policies, for example, is another evaluation element: when there is this loyalty, we are dealing with a behavior that is to be appreciated and therefore falls within the scope of the issues we are discussing. information on the supply chain is very important, as is, i believe, the preventive involvement of the social partners. stakeholders must be treated equally, with the same rights, and it is important that each of them feels involved in the relationship with the company. but it is clear that the social partners, the institutions on the one hand and the representatives of the workforce on the other, need preventive and systematic information. it is very useful that the european label of social responsibility has been proposed: we must reward those who choose to commit themselves to this aspect and do so with loyalty to their partners. finally, i would like to say that i find the proposal in the reports to urge the commission to come forward with a legislative proposal on non-financial information for companies very interesting. in times of difficulty such as the one we are going through, when a company is in difficulty because it has no productive activity, because it is suffering the effects of the crisis, if it has provided timely information on its health, if it has given all its interlocutors the information to know, it will be easier to manage any restructuring process. so a piece of legislation that makes this a well-established practice can be the next positive development we are facing.
