in writing. - i voted in favour of this important resolution which clearly and decisively reaffirms the support for women, especially in this period of economic crisis. women are the most discriminated against, especially in the workplace. the issue of reconciling work and private and family life must remain a priority, despite the difficult times we are living through and we must never let our guard down. it is enough to consider that the fall in the birth rate in the eu is undoubtedly exacerbated by the increase in unemployment and the precariousness and uncertainty of the future, which are profoundly undermining our society. the member states and the eu must make every effort to help women through concrete aid and policies that are appropriate and increasingly coordinated with each other to better achieve the result. i also fully agree with the call on the european commission to review the gender pay gap directive, as already requested by parliament in a 2012 resolution. equal pay for men and women for equal work or work of equal value is a matter of social justice which must be guaranteed without reservation.
in writing. − the austerity and budgetary policies of the european union have not only had a negative effect on the macroeconomic factors of the member states, but have also contributed to the widening of social and gender gaps. our group, and the italian delegation i have the honour to represent, have repeatedly stressed the need to reverse course and have repeatedly urged the heads of state and government to try to reach an agreement on the budget, which would not be limited to the short and medium term but would try to look to the future of the next generations and to the need to deliver a europe that is truly united and in solidarity. in this context, the position of women - in the workplace and in society - must and can only be improved by adopting policies that make innovation and investment their common denominator.
in writing. - i gave a positive opinion on the report on the impact of the economic crisis on gender equality and women's rights, because during the economic crisis which has hit europe in recent years, women have suffered from a precariousness of work, which has resulted in the predominant growth of atypical forms of work. women are also often forced to leave work to care for children or elderly family members. this has a profound impact on their career path. the situation is even more critical in the peripheral areas of the eu, where, however, member states should exploit the enormous amounts of alternative forms of energy to create jobs, for example in the 'green' sector (solar or wind energy), and reduce female unemployment. in addition, the crisis has also hit single parents hard, who, due to the need for atypical working hours, have increased the risk of poverty for women. in order to try to stem the effects of the crisis, it is necessary for the european institute for gender equality in vilnius to monitor the consequences of the crisis and its effects on the female labour market, in order to eliminate any form of discrimination in the recruitment process and to ensure equal rights for women in the labour market.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution. the world economy has been hit by a series of successive crises - financial, economic and now social - which have particularly affected women. european women are being hit by a crisis that is more silent than that affecting men, but no less tragic. for example, women in the public sector represent on average almost 70% of the workforce and are the main victims of budget cuts by member state governments. the reduction in public employees reached 25% in some member states. in 2011, 31.6% of women worked part-time. the phenomenon has now reached such proportions that the european commission does not speak of parttime work but of parttime unemployment. it is therefore essential to integrate the gender perspective into the solutions that the institutions will define to address the crisis.
in writing. - european women are affected by a silent crisis and although the effects of the crisis have been felt more slowly and less violently than men, they are still present. it is therefore essential to integrate the gender perspective into the solutions that the public authorities will define to address the crisis. i am not in agreement with all the points in the proposal, but i voted in favour of it because i believe that the european social fund must be mobilised, along with all the other european programmes, to promote greater social inclusion of women through improved vocational integration.
in writing. − the global crisis that began in 2008 has led governments to focus their efforts on fiscal consolidation, forgetting the social crisis that has been fuelled by the combination of economic crises, which is particularly affecting european women. the consequences on women have been felt more subtly, more silently, the effects of the crisis have been felt more slowly and less violently than on men, but in the long run they will pay the highest price, as cuts in public services will affect women's work more permanently. it is necessary to establish without delay a common framework of rules regarding the use of the european social entrepreneurship fund, with particular reference to the eligible investment objectives, the investment instruments they may use and the categories of investors who may invest in those funds.
in writing. − we are all aware of the financial crisis that has been plaguing the european union since 2008, but little is said about the serious social consequences it has brought. first of all unemployment, and particularly female unemployment. in the initial period of the crisis, men were the most affected by job loss, but as additional problems such as the decline in public services and the decline in household spending power took place, women were in many cases forced to leave their jobs, which had already been transformed from full-time to part-time contracts, to enter the informal economy. the combination of these events has contributed to the sharpening of gender inequality as a consequence of the economic crisis. it is therefore essential that measures for post-crisis economic recovery also include education and training policies which enable women to adapt to the evolution of the labour market. a good idea is to use the european social fund to stimulate and encourage women's reintegration into the world of work, and to develop gender equality policies in all aspects of the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework. i therefore express my favourable opinion.
mr president, a few months ago the european commission adopted the proposal for a directive on the so-called 'pink quotas'. i don't like the term, i prefer "equal democracy". the debate, vote and adoption of this measure will be a useful test of the goodwill of this parliament, the commission and above all the member states to help eliminate those stereotypes which still affect so many women in their professional careers and which we have identified in this resolution, which i voted in favour of. however, it is disconcerting to hear that an important and powerful woman, the german chancellor, is opposing the possibility of so-called "pink quotas" on boards of directors, a sign that there is clearly still a long way to go, especially since this is a woman who is interrupting a virtuous path in the process of overcoming stereotypes about women. i would also ask that the alarm caused by these statements be brought to light as soon as possible.
in writing. - the disparities between men and women in terms of socioeconomic conditions remain deeply rooted in the traditional gender role-based division, which places men primarily in charge of generating income and women in charge of providing care for the home and family free of charge. women are victims of cultural discrimination that does not take into account meritocracy: the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to apply the principle of equal treatment to women in the same way as to men. the cultural misperception that makes women vulnerable to discrimination and violence must be reversed, including through the responsible use of information media and new technologies, and the threshold for women's participation in political and economic decision-making must be raised.
in writing. − i voted for this report because, despite the eu’s commitments, there is still a gap in legislation on non-discrimination against women and gender equality in the areas of social security, education, media, employment and wages. women continue to be under-represented in political decision-making at local, national and eu level. most of all, gender stereotypes and sexism are still prevalent in both political and economic decision-making bodies, with regular instances of sexist remarks and harassment, including some forms of sexual harassment and violence against women. in addition to that, in almost every eu member state many women continue to carry a disproportionate share of the burden when it comes to raising children and taking care of other dependants. this is due to the persistence of stereotypes which act as a barrier to the sharing of family and domestic responsibilities between women and men and hinders the achievement of equality in the labour market.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mrs liotard on the elimination of gender stereotypes in the european union. gender stereotypes also arise from the lack of female representation in certain positions, which are still perceived as only "male". only by reversing this trend can the current prejudices that limit women's opportunities and choices in the social, economic and political spheres be broken down.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution because of the political message which draws attention to gender inequality. the fourth world conference on women was held in beijing on 15 september 1995, at which the declaration and platform for action on the "removal of all obstacles to the active participation of women in all areas of public and private life" were adopted. however, after more than 15 years, gender stereotypes and inequalities are still common problems in the european union today. women are often underrepresented in the media, or are portrayed in roles considered 'feminine', with the result that even greater gender discrimination is encouraged in a number of sectors of society and across all age groups. this trend must be reversed, especially by taking action to prevent the phenomenon from occurring in the cultural sphere, but without prior censorship of information media which operate with due regard for the protection of the younger public. i therefore felt that i had to take account of the need not to impose any censorship on adult citizens in relation to content they access, as long as such content does not violate the rights of minors, while hoping that the role of women will be better protected against gender discrimination and exploitation which certainly have a cultural base in pornography.
in writing. − whereas gender equality is a fundamental human right. guaranteed by the eu, in accordance with article 8 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, 'the union shall aim, in all its actions, to eliminate inequalities and to promote equality between men and women'; whereas the prevalence of negative gender stereotypes based on social prejudices and attitudes is also harmful to women and limits their opportunities and choices in the social, economic and political spheres; i voted in favour of the proposal despite some points of disagreement, aware that to tackle the problem of the lack of women at the highest levels of economic and political decision-making, we must tackle the persistence of gender stereotypes at all levels of society.
in writing. − gender equality is a fundamental human right and to achieve it the european union must continue to work to eliminate all forms of inequality by promoting equality between men and women. the fourth world conference on women held in beijing in 1995 must remain the reference point in this respect for the removal of all obstacles to women's active participation in public and private life. this must be the starting point and the end point for all our actions now and in the future.
in writing. − many of the european union's major objectives relate to social policies, in particular the elimination of all discrimination on grounds of gender, race or religion. on the elimination of gender discrimination, since 1995, with the adoption of the beijing declaration and platform for action, the european union has committed itself to constantly monitoring progress and implementing resolutions on women's rights. however, despite the constant renewal of the available means, there remains an objective gender inequality, which is reflected in the world of work, with different levels of contributions but also in the economic and political decision-making environment. therefore, there is a need to persevere in the implementation of positive practices and teachings from the media and schools that help to train new generations free from gender stereotypes and discrimination. i therefore express a favourable opinion.
in writing. - the report by mr rossi, 'making the most of eu environmental measures', was put to the vote after the rapporteurs from the main groups of the ppe, s&d, alde and greens/efa had agreed on a long series of amendments with the sole purpose of distorting the content of the entire report, which is why i voted against it.
in writing. - i supported this resolution because potential endocrine disruptors include substances such as steroid hormones, certain pesticides, dioxins, and plastic additives. as there are still questions to be answered, we have therefore asked the commission to take action to protect human health, particularly the health of vulnerable groups such as the elderly, pregnant women and children.
in writing. − this report, in the spirit of smart regulation, is an attempt to consolidate efforts to improve the implementation of european environmental legislation, by leveraging on the simplification of eu environmental law, reducing administrative burdens and strengthening european and national administrative structures. the aim is to embark on a path towards effective implementation of european environmental legislation through the development of evidence-based policies and strategies, with the cooperation of the member states and local authorities. it is a question of taking up the challenge of subsidiarity, of bringing environmental legislation into a closer relationship with citizens and national administrations, increasing its immediacy and transparency. i regret that my shadow rapporteurs agreed to a long series of amendments with the intention of making a fundamental change to the report without even consulting me. despite this unfair procedure, i shall vote in favour of the text, even though i have some doubts about it.
in writing. − the european union has developed considerable legislation on environmental protection. one of the major obstacles we face is the ineffective implementation of these provisions at national, regional and local level. the report by mr rossi proposes the elimination of many administrative and bureaucratic obstacles: the savings in economic terms would therefore amount to eur 50 billion per year. this measure can only benefit the european industry. environmental protection is not just a matter for businesses, but has a considerable impact on the lives of all citizens. i believe it is important to increase the levels of transparency and to inform european citizens adequately about the content and the effects, including legal ones, that these policies have on their daily lives.
in writing. − much of european legislation takes the form of directives which, by setting out general guidelines, leave member states a wide margin of discretion as to how they implement them. it is important, however, that all community directives are correctly transposed and implemented in accordance with the guidelines specifically laid down for environmental matters. according to the latest data, the annual cost of non-implementation of eu environmental legislation is currently €50 billion in direct health and environmental costs, not including the negative effects on the state of the environment in the eu. to prevent this from happening, all member states must be urged to adopt a responsible approach to environmental policy and to respect the correct use of environmental policy, ensuring a proper flow of information and transparency. this will require increased monitoring and control and more frequent collection of updated data, including, where necessary, the establishment of an environmental law inspection unit to monitor and assist in the implementation of environmental legislation. i am in favour of this.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to thank all the shadow rapporteurs, the secretariat, the individual rapporteurs who contributed to the drafting of the report and the drafting of the compromise amendments, and all the staff who supported us. it is clear that we are on the eve of an important stage for this parliament, which is taking a position for the first time in a legislative body on the common agricultural policy. what i really hope is that tomorrow's vote will be the fruit of a lot of hard work, which has seen us participate in a new process, but also in a different context, for which i, together with my fellow rapporteurs, have proposed possible solutions and keys capable of opening up opportunities for european farmers in a global economic context which still sees them in great difficulty and suffering. we are committed to them and, although other voices are more prominent than theirs, we have worked to respond to their problematic requests, which have been plaguing farmers for too long, by making them an active part of the definition of a really effective cap with really measurable results. the report by mr ashworth and mr deß has already confirmed parliament's willingness and commitment to simplify the complex administrative machinery and reduce the burden on farmers, including for the common agricultural policy after 2013. the time has come to put that will into practice by developing and putting in place simple instruments that will foster greater compliance at all levels in a still uncertain financial environment. in my proposal i have tried to sum up some of the important points of what has been agreed so far, and to put into practice some of the real requirements: the first is simplification, which is done in many ways. for example, by means of a multiannual application with annual confirmation; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not affected by the crisis. we also need to distinguish between fraud and non-compliance, and this is a great step forward for all honest farmers whom we must protect, but also for a system of controls which we must streamline. as regards the penalties for greening, the proposed amendment to article 65 of the text is, in my view, designed to ensure that the administrative penalties for greening payments do not go beyond those payments and therefore do not affect the basic payment. i think that this need must be clearly stated in order to avoid misunderstandings and to open the way to possible difficulties for farmers in the first phase of the new common agricultural policy. the role of the member states in the implementation of the new cap will be important through the renewed management of control and certification systems, which lead to a reduction in error rates as well as the number of on-the-spot checks, thus rewarding the most virtuous states. as far as rural development is concerned, i referred to the so-called automatic decommitment of regional development programmes, in order to give the possibility that resources which a region has failed to spend in its own rdp may remain in the member state and be redistributed to more virtuous regions. mr president, these are just some of the many measures proposed to make the procedures and criteria for allocating resources transparent. i have to say one last thing about the subject of transparency, which has been discussed by a number of other colleagues. the publication of data on beneficiaries under the current financial regulation is mandatory for all. i would like to see farmers not be burdened with additional costs compared with those who benefit from all the other structural funds. that is why i naturally ask that the general rule be applied to all and that there be no greater burdens and constraints on farmers than on others.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in bananas. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on regional policy, i am pleased to be able to contribute to the adoption of the general regulation on the cap, an instrument which guides agricultural policies towards the europe 2020 strategy. that is why the regi committee has opted for a horizontal regulation based on effectiveness and efficiency and addressing the needs of farmers and rural communities, including those on the outskirts and on the margins, in order to have a greener and fairer cap, while maintaining greening as the first pillar, a cap that is nonetheless rigorous, in order to ensure long-term sustainability and the interoperability of resources and structures. the regulation promotes sustainable, smart and less bureaucratic farming, which ensures real and effective environmental measures and reduces the gap between farmers who have received resources on the basis of historical expenditure in the past.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we have found many good solutions in the committee on agriculture and rural development. the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. the fact is that in recent years some member states, e.g. germany, have done their homework and moved away from the historical premium towards a regional approach. in most countries, including the country i come from - in italy - this has not happened. there, the average premium in the regions where farming is most difficult, namely in the mountains, is 50 euros per hectare, and just 100 kilometres away, where farming is easier in the plain, it is 500 euros. that's a ratio of 1:10 in a very small space. worse still, where premiums are highest, many farmers have de facto withdrawn from farming and live off the fact that they receive good premiums and generate income. i often say that whereas we used to have couch potatoes -- these were farmers who had milk quotas and then sold them and lived off of them -- we now have couch bonus recipients. so these are premium recipients who are living off the fact that they have historical premium rights and there's little farming behind it. we must improve on this point. i would also ask you, commissioner, to do everything possible to ensure that the period of the financial framework, that is to say the next seven years, is used to finally create equality among farmers here.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased with the work done in the committee on agriculture, which has improved on the proposal originally put forward by commissioner cioloş and which, in our view, contained genuinely punitive measures for agriculture, such as greening which increased bureaucracy, such as immediate convergence, which would have brought whole crops and whole areas of europe to their knees, without taking account of the diversity of our agriculture. the proposal which emerges from the vote in the committee on agriculture guarantees flexibility in convergence and guarantees those who today receive the direct payment as a result of the historical premium a minimum and diluted loss over time: i am thinking of olive groves, tomatoes, arable land in some parts of my country, such as southern italy. we are therefore pleased that the cap is focusing on a number of essential issues: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the conclusion of the agreement on the european economic area, which is to be signed by the council and the commission on 1 january. we are concerned, commissioner, about the budget cuts. we need resources to protect and support quality agriculture, to recognise and promote the value of production, to guarantee the dignity of farmers' incomes. we will give a strong mandate for the negotiations tomorrow but we are prepared to vote against if the negotiations do not meet parliament's demands and if adequate resources are not identified to support agriculture and farmers.
member of the commission. - mr president, thank you all for this lively debate. i conclude that we agree on the objectives and principles of this reform. and this is quite normal, since the debate and preparation of this reform has been going on for years. there are also areas where i see that we are in agreement, at least from what i have heard here today. of course, we'll see what the votes say tomorrow. but in any case, i could see that we were in favour of an agriculture which was more in line with the optimal management of natural resources, that the first pillar of the cap should contribute to the achievement of this objective, that we were in favour of an equivalence between the agri-environmental measures of the second pillar and other environmental practices, of an equivalence system which is therefore credible and simple to apply, of greening which should have a positive impact on all agricultural areas, and of a credible system of penalties to ensure the effectiveness of this type of greening. i also understand that you support a common agricultural policy which is transparent, because i think we all believe that the cap is effective, useful and that therefore we have nothing to hide, that we can show the taxpayers what the community's money is for. i also understood that you were in favour of a fairer common agricultural policy, providing for a better distribution of aid between the member states, but also within the member states, between farmers, and that therefore, even taking into account certain specificities in certain member states and regions, where the process of equivalence should take more time and be done in stages, we should eventually arrive at real convergence. i have also heard those of you who support the idea of should like to say a word about the less-favoured areas. in my view and in the commission's view, we must have a targeted tool to direct aid towards less favoured areas, but we must also take into account the fact that today in europe more than 140 different criteria are used to define less favoured areas. that is why we think it is important to be able to take a decision now, in the context of the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr trzaskowski has already made it clear that our aim was to fulfil a very delicate task which the treaty assigns to us and which is made necessary by the imminent accession of croatia to the union and by the end of the derogation to the ceiling of 751 members in force until the end of the current term of office, and to do so in a serious and responsible manner, by presenting a proposal which is based on the principle of degressive proportionality laid down in the treaty and at the same time declines it in a pragmatic and realistic way. as you know, the proposal is based on two stages: the first of these attempts to faithfully decline the three principles which this house voted for in the lamassoure-severin report, namely: a larger country is entitled to a greater number of seats, a member of parliament from a larger country must represent a greater number of citizens than a member from a smaller country, and it is also important to remember this third principle, namely that the maximum and minimum thresholds of 96 and 6 seats respectively should be used. the result of this first stage is a significant redistribution of seats, which we therefore consider unrealistic and inappropriate at this time. hence the second stage, which results from a political compensation carried out precisely, as rafał said, on the basis of the double principle 'no one gains and no one loses more than one seat'. it is a balanced and politically viable outcome, as has been demonstrated by the very broad support for the proposal in the committee on constitutional affairs, and we hope that this will be reflected in the vote in the house tomorrow. this does not mean, of course, that it is a perfect proposal: but i think it can be described as the least imperfect of the possible solutions. the vote tomorrow will also decide whether the last seat should be ceded by sweden, as in the original proposal, or by austria, as the afco committee has decided. i am aware of the sensitivity of the issue for both countries, which will, however, in any case elect at least one more member of parliament in 2014 than in 2009. the logic of the two-stage solution would lead to sweden being asked to make the sacrifice, whereas an assessment that does not take into account the first stage may support the opposite reasoning. i am personally, of course, fond of the original proposal, but in any case i feel that whatever the house decides on this point, the coherence and soundness of the whole proposal will not be affected. it would therefore be good if the european council adopted parliament's proposal without introducing amendments, which would inevitably trigger a veto mechanism. and i think i can say that the rapporteur's approach is to not give our consent to solutions other than those which will be voted on in this house. finally, i would like to stress the importance of another element in the resolution, namely parliament's commitment to propose a seat allocation mechanism in the context of a more general revision of the treaties, which also addresses the issue of the voting system in the council and also reopens the question of the introduction of a transnational list. these are two crucial points which should not be avoided but which must be dealt with appropriately in what we hope will be a constituent legislature for european democracy. we believe that this report and the solutions it proposes and indicates are a contribution in this direction and we therefore ask all members to support it with conviction.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the two rapporteurs, who have done a very difficult and lengthy job, without refraining from making some general and broader remarks. we are on a path in which europe pursues three objectives: the european parliament has been a very active participant in the process of european integration, and it has been a very active participant in the process of european integration. the synthesis is not so easy: in particular, the democratic principle would require that the decision-making power of each individual citizen be identical and that therefore each member of parliament represent an identical number of voters. but this would make the smaller states disappear and give the larger states excessive dominance. that is why the treaty of lisbon speaks of degressive proportionality, which the afco committee has interpreted to mean that in no case should the population of the states be put in order and that no representation of a state should be higher than that of a state with a larger population. the pragmatic solution which is being put forward today is concerned with determining the minimum sacrifice and the minimum advantage for the states which have to sacrifice or improve their representation as a result of croatia's accession. the afco committee has been trying for a long time to find mathematical formulas that could be used in the future for new entrants. but no automatic solution has been found so far. it is therefore clear that we are asking the states which are losing seats to contribute to european integration, but at the same time we should like to see further reflection on this subject, which could lead to a revision of the treaties in the future. in the meantime, progress is being made and it is hoped that there will be no obstacles to delay final approval. there will be a way later, including through a possible reform of the treaties, to examine the whole case more broadly. that is why i believe that all the amendments, even if some of them are very good, should be rejected and that the text proposed by the committee should be accepted with conviction.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank all the members who have spoken, who have made their contribution and who have also shown how difficult our task was. i should like to begin by thanking the colleagues from those countries who, in accepting mr rangel's invitation, understood the spirit, the logic and the rationality of the proposal, even though they lost a seat on the basis of it, and thus contributed to the successful outcome of the first stage of a procedure which is certainly complex and difficult. i think the discussion has highlighted the reasons for the complexity of the task entrusted to us: european democracy - it is good for everyone to remember this - is based on the principle of dual representation of citizens and states, and this principle is made even more complex by the fact that it is not realistically possible to distribute these two principles and have one of the two chambers representing citizens in a proportional manner and another representing the states. these two principles must coexist in a difficult balance within each of the two houses - parliament and council - but also in the relationship between them, a balance which cannot be established only in an abstract and unilateral way but which is also the result of a historical process of accumulation of weights and balances, which have in some way linked the allocation of a certain number of seats to parliament and that of a certain weight within the council. it is therefore a complex and multifaceted reality, and i would urge all colleagues to be cautious, even in their statements. mr werthmann has called for a mathematical solution: i would remind you that the main mathematical solutions - both the cambridge proposal and the parabolic proposal - which we have also included in our annex, would have meant that your country, austria, would have had to cut three members of parliament. so be careful about invoking mathematics. at the same time, i would like to say to the colleagues from the larger countries, who in some ways are also legitimately calling for an increase in seats, that this debate should have shown them that the problem, mr bélier, is not the unanimity of the european council, but the ability of this parliament to find a synthesis within itself and not to rely simply on the logic of the larger countries imposing the strength of numbers on the smaller ones. the problem is to find a solution of broad consensus, and i think that the principle that 'no one gains and no one loses more than one seat' is in the end the least imperfect of all possible principles, and any other solution which may seem better from an individual and unilateral point of view, when seen in the wider context of this house, in which we are all represented, is much more problematic than the one we are proposing. the question of austria and sweden, which has been the subject of much discussion in this debate, remains. i really respect and understand the positions of the representatives of both countries, i understand the sensitivity of the problem, but i would like to remind you - not to de-dramatise the matter but to remind you of a fact - that both austria and sweden have won two more seats in any case and that therefore, whatever happens in the vote tomorrow, neither country will elect less than one more member of parliament than the previous time. so there will still be an increase compared to the 2009 elections. that does not of course take away the fact that no one is excited about losing a seat, and i understand that. i repeat that the question can be considered from two points of view: the commission has already made a number of proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to accept them. this is the logical consequence of the two-step model. but i also recognize... (the president interrupts the speaker)
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i should like to begin by thanking mrs westlund for this important report which we are supporting. for some 20 years we have seen a steady increase in hormonal disorders and diseases caused by endocrine disruptors, substances capable of dangerously altering the proper functioning of our endocrine system. thousands of studies and research studies have been carried out worldwide, identifying these substances as one of the main causes of such diseases as reproductive disorders, premature puberty, breast cancer, but also foetal malformations, cases of diabetes and many others. endocrine disruptors are unfortunately found almost everywhere: in food packaging, cosmetics, electronic equipment, building materials, furniture, textiles, toys, and all these products, in our daily use, are released into the environment where they accumulate, for example, in the dust in our homes. this situation particularly exposes certain more vulnerable groups, such as women of childbearing age and small children who crawle on the floor and tend to put their fingers in their mouths. if we are to strengthen research in this field, we must also act on the legislative front and apply the precautionary principle, which is one of the cornerstones of the european union's chemicals policy. as with bisphenol a, which is now banned in the manufacture of baby bottles, we must restrict the use of these substances and adapt all relevant european legislation, namely the reach regulation, the directives on labelling and packaging, biocides and cosmetics. protecting the health of european citizens and creating a healthier living environment around them is our imperative duty.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, as you have heard, we are faced with two facts which should guide our action. the first is that hormonal disorders are on the increase and a substantial part of these are related to the effect of endocrine disruptors. the second is that science, unfortunately, still has quite limited levels of knowledge on the subject. so we have to do two things: the first is to give practical effect to the precautionary principle. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the most vulnerable people, from children to women who decide to become mothers, are properly protected. the second is to encourage all research activities quickly, because we cannot afford to lose time. what we do not see is very dangerous, but the effects that we do see are of the kind described in mrs westlund's report.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, let me react to the main topics in your debate. firstly, preparations for the european council. it is clear that the european economy will be the prime topic for discussion in the european council. i would really like to reassure honourable members that the commission is pursuing exactly the track many of you have been calling for. this is clearly growth-friendly consolidation, support for growth and restoration of our economic competitiveness. most of us agree that fiscal consolidation is necessary. clear efforts in this regard brought us back from the abyss of the euro implosion which was expected and forecast by many just a year ago. we want to do this in a manner that takes into account reality and at the same time lays the ground for future growth. we are basing our policies on structural deficits, taking into account consolidation efforts, structural reforms and the external environment as well. as we have shown in the past with several member states, we are ready to give member states more time to consolidate their budgets if they are making a real effort and if the structural reforms are implemented. the commission will push strongly to use all the growth levers we have at our disposal. the eib has had its basic capital increased, so this bank will be allowed to provide eur 180 billion more in loans in the next three years. we have completed the preparation for project bonds where, again, more than eur 4.5 billion could be invested in infrastructure projects. we are reallocating the money from the esf and other funds to support the creation of jobs for youth and the long-term unemployed. we will also push – and here we believe we will have your strong support – for making better use of the single market potential. we still have quite a serious implementation gap in implementing the measures which we know will bring growth and the creation of new jobs to the european union. nevertheless, if you look at our track record with single market acts 1 and 2, there is a lot to do and we will be making as much effort as much as possible to ensure that we can benefit better from the single market. some of you referred to the forecast and questioned the methodology used by the commission, but please compare our forecast with those of the oecd, the ecb or the imf. you will find that it was usually the commission which was closest to reality. the crisis is unprecedented and has many new features. therefore, forecasting is also very difficult. on the multiannual financial framework, we are expecting your vote in a few moments. we respect your prerogative and we are greatly encouraged by the clear statement by the irish presidency to start comprehensive negotiations with you. the commission – president barroso, commissioner lewandowski and i – will do our utmost to be helpful and creative and to help the legislators find agreement on mff. we all know how much europe and european citizens need it. on hungary, i would like to assure parliament that recent developments are being closely followed by the commission. they were raised by president barroso with the hungarian prime minister just a few days ago. he assured him that hungary is fully committed to eu values and eu law. it was in that respect that the joint statement with the secretary-general of the council of europe, mr jagland, was issued. i would of course also like to reassure you that the commission, in very close cooperation with the council of europe and its venice commission, will proceed with a detailed analysis of the recent steps. as you have seen on many occasions, the commission treats all member states fairly, but at the same time always stands very firmly for full respect for european principles and law. this will be the case again. once again the commission will not hesitate to use all the instruments at its disposal once the analysis is finalised, and if necessary to ask for, and insist upon, the changes to be made by the hungarian authorities. i would like to conclude on a very serious note. this morning we heard in this chamber a statement associating two nations with crime. we heard suggestions that political decisions should be made on the assumption that romanians and bulgarians are bringing crime to the european union. this is stigmatisation, this is against all principles of non-discrimination and this is against european values. this statement has very clear xenophobic features. on behalf of the commission, i reject this statement and this approach. i am sure that this house will support us in this as well.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i think this has been a very helpful and a very interesting debate, and i want to say that the irish presidency has been following very carefully parliament’s deliberations on the mff, not just through this debate but for quite some time. the resolution on the mff – and the debate with so many contributions today right across the political spectrum – makes parliament’s position very clear. this usefully prepares the ground for our upcoming negotiations. i believe that there are grounds to go towards meeting some of parliament’s concerns; for example in relation to the question of flexibility and of, perhaps, a mid-term review, which has been mentioned by many speakers and which is reflected in the resolution. i need to make clear to the house the council’s view that the european council in february produced a solid outcome and was at the limit of what was possible at that meeting. i would also mention that this council outcome in february was the result of almost two years of deliberations at the general affairs council, and again in consultation with the european parliament. it is not something that appeared overnight, but rather something that was the product of very intensive and very extensive negotiations between the member states. in a period of huge budgetary austerity, there is only a marginal reduction in real terms on the current mff – itself agreed in much better times. there is a substantial increase, some 37%, in spending on competitiveness and research. i know that a range of members today have specifically focused on the need to enhance provision for research and development. therefore, i think that is a significant feature in the proposal. many members have rightly pointed to the massive challenge that we face in respect of unemployment, particularly youth unemployment. that is why i believe that the eur 6 billion figure allocated for the youth employment initiative is extremely important and timely. cohesion policy and the common agricultural policy, which are of enormous importance to many member states and many regions throughout the eu, have been largely preserved. as i mentioned, the taoiseach, our prime minister, has already met twice with president schulz since the european council to discuss how we can best move forward. they have agreed to maintain very close and regular contact and i expect that they will hold discussions again tomorrow at the european council. the tánaiste, our deputy prime minister, who is the chairman of the general affairs council, will continue negotiations, along with myself, on behalf of the council. we are in regular contact with the contact group here in parliament, with the group leaders and with the conference of committee chairs, and we will indeed build on this contact. we have a really important window of opportunity now to engage intensively on these issues in the weeks ahead. i very much welcome the statement from the commission in respect of parliament’s commitment to engage and to support that process. emerging from the debate here today, the message now has to be that we have no time to waste; that we have to move forward swiftly and with a sense of determination to arrive at a successful conclusion in these negotiations between the council and parliament. on the sectoral legislation – agriculture, cohesion etc – the presidency will aim to make the maximum possible progress with its opposite numbers in parliament. we will be constructive partners with the aim of achieving first reading agreements on as many mff-related files as possible within the irish presidency, in other words by the end of june. clearly, good progress on the mff will assist in this and i know that parliament shares this goal. we look forward to working closely with you on that. with the spring european council concluding the first phase of the european semester 2013, i think it is appropriate that i conclude by acknowledging again the very important work of the european parliament towards enhancing the democratic legitimacy of our collective efforts to support competitiveness, growth and jobs. i refer in particular to the parliamentary week of the european semester at the end of january and the development of a stronger dialogue with national parliaments, which i think we can all agree is extremely important. the irish presidency has been keen to support all of these efforts. it is clear from last year’s lessons-learned exercise that the european semester should be an open and inclusive process, supporting meaningful engagement with parliaments and all of the relevant stakeholders, both at european and at national level. these are therefore important contributions to an important debate, and provide a very strong basis for further reflection and engagement over the period ahead. it is clear that strong economic governance arrangements must go hand in hand with stronger democratic legitimacy, and that is a principle which the irish presidency holds very dear and will continue to promote. we must also, of course, remain firmly focused on the scale of the current jobs crisis. i have already alluded to the scourge of youth unemployment, as many members have in your debate today. unemployment levels are up on this time last year and are unacceptably high: now at almost 12% for the euro area, and 11% for the eu as a whole. there is no stronger signal that we must redouble our efforts towards economic recovery. we cannot realistically claim to have emerged from the current crisis until our economies are growing again and, most importantly, our economies are creating jobs for our citizens. ms podimata actually summed this up extremely well when she said that we must once again regain the trust of our citizens. this is the litmus test for that. to regain the trust of our citizens we have to give them hope; we have to show them that there is a future which can be guided and delivered by the european union, by all eu member states and the european institutions working together to deal with that. a number of members referred to the need for a two-track process. i agree with this. i think we need to focus on consolidation, but coupling that with a firm focus on the growth agenda. i would firmly disagree with the idea that these are somehow mutually exclusive. these are very clearly two sides of the same coin. we must stabilise public finances, we must deal with the mounting debt burden and we must not ignore the huge challenge of enormous deficits in member states if we are to tackle the challenge of competitiveness of growth and ultimately fulfil our commitment to delivering on the job creation agenda. we must focus firmly on both tracks, which of course are essential in terms of complementing each other. i would like to simply thank members once again for your attention and for a very stimulating debate. i sincerely look forward to working very closely with the european parliament on the mff in particular, to ensure that we have an outcome which delivers for our citizens and which delivers on our goal of regaining the trust of our citizens and of offering a bright future for our citizens. i think that is the role and responsibility of members of the european parliament, of members of the council and indeed of the commission, all working together to achieve that same objective. the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are voting today on a measure of extraordinary importance, relating to an area which is very close to the heart of the european parliament. the social economy is a crucial element for the identity and sustainability of the european social model. the social economy, and in particular the mutual funds, by combining profitability and solidarity, play a key role, creating quality jobs and local employment, generating social capital and promoting active citizenship. a welfare based on solidarity is a type of economy that respects democratic values, putting the human person first. in the face of the challenges posed by the economic and financial crisis, mutual societies are providing vital and sustainable responses to growth, employment and social cohesion by providing affordable healthcare, social services and insurance to over 160 million european citizens, creating an estimated 350 000 jobs and helping to identify concrete solutions to reform welfare systems and the social economy. all of this deserves recognition and political investment. the fundamental theme of europe at this moment is growth, which is being invoked by everyone. there can be no growth without the contribution of the social economy, which is an essential part of it. if we are calling for growth, we cannot ignore this sector, which is why i am calling for a general value for a particular sector such as the social economy and therefore for recognition throughout europe. mutual funds have a role to play in these challenges alongside the private sector and must be able to compete on equal terms with other forms of enterprise in the union, which the existing european statutes, such as the cooperative and the european company statutes, cannot exhaust due to differences in governance models. and here we come to the second aspect, the second central theme of europe today, which is its integration, its march towards political unity and its enlargement of the internal market. in this respect too, today's measure emphasizes a general value, which comes from the field of mutual funds and thus acquires relevance for the whole of europe. parliament has already supported the european commission's efforts to adopt a regulation on the statute of the european mutual fund. after the impasse in the council and the withdrawal of the commission's first proposal, we are now again calling for a legal instrument for mutual societies to facilitate their crossborder activities and complete the internal market, and we are calling on the commission to proceed decisively in this direction after parliament's decision today. we will continue to press, together with the whole world of mutual aid, this house, this parliament, to ensure that the european institutions are the bearers of the desired result. the proposed european statute therefore constitutes a voluntary instrument supplementary to the existing national rules applicable to mutual societies and would therefore not affect the existing statutes but would rather constitute a twenty-eighth regime which would make it easier for mutual societies to engage in cross-border activities.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank you for giving me this opportunity to participate in this interesting discussion on the subject of promoting mutual societies. as i said in my introductory statement, not all the countries of europe have a mutualist tradition. clearly, this means that we have to consider ways of coping with the challenges faced by mutualist societies wishing to trade beyond their national borders. the most popular idea put forward is to adopt a statute for a european mutual society, so as to expand the mutualist movement in europe. nevertheless, it is important, at the same time, to enhance the visibility of the movement and not to neglect efforts to improve understanding of the way it operates. the results of the consultation which we launched will constitute the basis for thorough consideration of the need for, and thrust of, new policy initiatives and of the need for a proposal to introduce a european study. let me say that, for the commission, the european statute remains a viable option. i would like to ask all mutualist organisations to reply to the consultation questionnaire. the commission will certainly also draw on the berlinguer report and the contributions made by all the honourable members, whose pleas i will convey to commissioner tajani.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr commissioner, cotton is a truly unique product. it's a raw material that's indispensable, that we wear every day: it's almost like a second skin. it is a product which we import and export in europe, which unfortunately involves a lot of child labour in developing countries, and we can recall that parliament refused to include a textile protocol in the trade agreement with uzbekistan, given the massive use of children in cotton harvesting in that country. it is a product that has a considerable, sometimes devastating, environmental impact with pesticides, insecticides and a huge use of water, which is necessary for the cultivation of the plantations, which also has remarkable, though small for the moment, examples of good fair and solidarity-based trade practices, which gives jobs to entire countries that depend on cotton - bangladesh, uzbekistan - but also to our textile industry, and which involves a very complex chain of responsibility, made up of producers, wholesalers, traders, brands, industries, consumers, even advertisers. it is therefore a product which needs a role for the legislator, for the government, for a system. and that is what i think our discussion should be focused on. we have the tools at our disposal today, as the commissioner has pointed out: the european union must first of all join the international cotton advisory committee, which is a gap that must be filled. secondly, we are working together on specific clauses in the economic partnership and free trade agreements. thirdly, we are working on new rules for granting the system of generalised preferences, subject to good governance and compliance with international conventions on labour and the environment. finally, we need constant monitoring, including through systematic partnership with un bodies such as unicef or the international labour organization. finally, we must find the link in a virtuous chain, remembering the un global compact and remembering that cotton was also synonymous with slavery. in the 21st century, we would like it to be synonymous with development.
