mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in february of this year the cracks in the already very delicate balance of the middle east question were violently reopened. this time the casus belli was the arrest of a 30-year-old palestinian, arafat jaradat, accused of throwing stones at israeli citizens. after a few days of interrogation in the prisons, the palestinian people were informed of the death of the boy, who, according to the israeli prison service, died of a heart attack. following an initial autopsy carried out by the institute of forensic medicine in israel, it was widely assumed that arafat was tortured during interrogation. the episode reignited a never-ending fire that led all palestinian prisoners to a hunger strike, as well as an attempt at revenge by an armed group linked to al-fatah, which launched a rocket into southern israel. in view of all this, and recalling that relations between europe and israel are based on respect for human rights and democratic principles, and stressing that respect for human rights and international humanitarian law is one of the values shared by the parties, i share the call on the state of israel to respect the right to life and health of palestinian prisoners and i hope for an objective and democratic investigation procedure to ensure an impartial truth.
member of the commission. − mr president, why did the commission propose the clarification of the eu emissions trading system directive in the first place? the basic idea of the eu ets is very simple: to make the right to pollute our climate a scarce resource that has a price, so that companies think more about how to reduce emissions and integrate the cost of doing so into their investment and operational decisions. because emissions rights can be traded, they will tend to end up with those businesses and factories that need them most for their activities and, therefore, are ready to pay the price if they need more than what they have received for free. do not forget that a lot of allowances are given out for free. this approach is cost-effective for society and was therefore designed to be a key tool in the eu’s efforts to meet its climate objectives. it was also meant to implement the ‘polluter pays’ principle enshrined in the treaty and to give companies in the eu’s internal market a level playing field. a level playing field, moreover, where you cannot beat your competitor simply by polluting more; where profitability is not just based on pushing the bill onto future generations, and where innovation in less-polluting processes and technologies is rewarded and pays off for companies, also in the short term. unfortunately, the system is not currently meeting all of these expectations, and there is one overriding reason for that: the economic crisis. the crisis has caused a fall in industrial production in the eu and thus in demand for allowances. this has resulted in the build-up of a huge, unexpected surplus of allowances that undermines the proper functioning of the system which, as i said, was designed to work through scarcity. in short, the protracted crisis has dramatically affected the eu ets – just as it has affected so many other areas of economic activity in europe. just as policy-makers and legislators in the past few years have been busy responding to the crisis and addressing its many negative impacts on our economy, so it is time to address the impacts it has on the european ets. i know some of you argue that the ets is a market and that we should, therefore, leave it alone. but in the case of a politically-created market set up through legislative action, such as the carbon market, policy-makers and legislators arguably have an even greater responsibility to act than in other markets if the assumptions on which their legislation was based have, meanwhile, fundamentally changed. may i remind you once again of the point that we have just heard mr groote concede, that it was actually this parliament that, in conjunction with the energy efficiency directive, asked the commission to tackle this situation? that is what we have been responding to, and i think that this parliament also has a responsibility now. that is why the commission has proposed clarifying the eu ets directive and the backloading of the sale of 900 million allowances to 2019 and 2020 as a short-term measure to avoid things getting even worse while we prepare for more lasting solutions. and that is why the commission has also put up for discussion a shortlist of options for structural measures that could provide a solution to the surplus in the medium term. but i wish to stress that backloading in itself – which is what we are discussing today – will have no effect whatsoever on the amount of free allowances given to our energy-intensive companies, or on the total amount of allowances put into circulation in the years 2013-2020, the third phase. after this introduction i will briefly comment on three issues involving some of the more specific key concerns that i know some of you have raised in the discussions. first, the concern that backloading would set a precedent for future intervention of the same nature. the commission understands this concern, and i can therefore be very clear on this point. we have never had any desire or intention of repeating this kind of exercise in the future, and that is also why the relevant amendments in this regard proposed by the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (envi) would be acceptable to the commission. secondly, as regards the concerns expressed about electricity prices and the risk of carbon leakage, the commission has analysed the expected impact of backloading in an impact assessment, including – to the extent feasible – on individual sectors. the assessment shows clearly that the impacts of backloading are expected to remain well within those projected by past analysis. let me stress this very clearly: backloading is expected to counteract any further fall in the carbon price in the short term, in other words to stop the bleeding. it will not bring the price – or the impact on the risk of carbon leakage – anywhere close to the levels expected and politically accepted before the crisis, when the legislation was adopted. today the carbon price is around eur 4. it was supposed at this time to be around eur 30, so do not tell us that the crisis is not impacting on the price. of course it is. this means that, even with backloading, the impact of the crisis will still be reflected in a considerably lower carbon price than originally expected. according to those who are most into this market – you can see it in the press as late as today – they expect that you will see a very limited increase in the price if this parliament adopts this proposal tomorrow. this brings me to my last point. the market urgently needs parliament as well as the council to approve the proposal. i hope that you will do so tomorrow, because the sooner we get clarity on backloading the better, so that we can focus on what really matters – for instance, the 2030 framework – and deliver the predictability that our industries also need for the medium and longer term. the backdrop to all this is that climate change is getting worse. the eu’s dependency on imported fossil fuels is increasing and so is, therefore, the bill we have to pay for our energy. this is not only bad for the climate, it is also bad for our economy, our competitiveness and our jobs. let me finally stress one particular aspect that is at stake and which should be of particular concern to members of this parliament and european policymakers. to a large extent, backloading is the decision about whether we continue to regulate power generation and industry at european level or whether we act as bystanders witnessing an increasing fragmentation of the regulatory landscape and the internal market. i appeal to you, as the european parliament, to support the european ets as a common european tool. the alternative to doing this is not that we then just have very cheap prices and then nothing else happens. no, the alternative to securing the european ets is a patchwork of 27 different national regulatory systems. it cannot be in the interest of the european parliament to go back to renationalised climate and energy policies when one of the successes you have been instrumental in achieving is a europeanised climate and energy policy. i really hope that those of you who are still in doubt will bear this in mind tomorrow. that is the real alternative; that is why we need the backloading done, and we need it to be carried through tomorrow.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. mr president, i represent the position taken by the committee on industry, research and energy, which, by a very large majority, rejected the proposal sent to us by the commission. the basis of our rejection is the strong conviction that we cannot intervene in a market which is designed to be free and whose mechanisms must be regulated by the natural fluctuation between supply and demand. but even more, the vote in the itre committee is based on the conviction that europe, which is going through a severe crisis, especially in the manufacturing and steel sectors, with severe job cuts and the closure of many companies, cannot support a new crisis tax. in fact, this vote represents the hope that withdrawing quotas from the market will lead to an increase in the cost of quotas. the itre committee believes that the priorities for europe at present are jobs and growth. we believe that we can best defend the european manufacturing sector by keeping the market as proposed two years ago and not intervening in the course of the work with choices not shared by the vast majority of producers. of course, this could raise the cost of electricity bills even further in a continent like europe where even today that cost weighs too heavily on our production compared to the rest of the world markets.
on behalf of the efd group. i am in complete agreement with mrs sartori, chairman of the committee on industry, research and energy. the proposal to amend the ets directive, as it is formulated, gives the commission a free hand to intervene in the auction mechanism, to manipulate the market for allowances with the aim of controlling, or even predetermining, the price of co2. in addition, the proposal underestimates or completely ignores the impact on manufacturing and in particular on electricity-intensive sectors such as steel, which are struggling to return to pre-crisis production levels. as the conclusions of the last international conference on climate change showed, any binding commitments by other large global emitters comparable to those in europe will not be implemented until perhaps 2020. any action which would unilaterally increase the european effort to reduce emissions already set for 2020 would therefore appear to be totally unjustified and unacceptable. the european union should move beyond the unilateral policy and regulatory approach to climate dumping, insisting on a tariff policy at the borders of the european union.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a greenpeace study on the decline of bees, published last week, once again stresses the need to protect these pollinators by banning chemicals, such as neonicotinoids, which threaten their existence. the future of bees is not only at stake, but also that of all citizens of the union: in fact, most of our food depends significantly on the work of insect pollinators, and without their valuable help, about a third of food crops would have to be pollinated by other means. recently, efsa, through extensive research and targeted testing, has also established the lethal effects of neonicotinoids on bees, even at low doses. despite this scientific evidence, on 15 march the agriculture ministers of the 27 member states failed to agree on the ban on neonicotinoids proposed by the european commission. the fight against the powerful pesticide lobby is therefore still very tough, but we must insist and achieve a europe without pesticides. it is a common sense decision and it is what the european citizens want.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, first of all let me thank the committee on international trade (inta) and its rapporteur, ms saïfi, for the work done in preparing this comprehensive report. for those who were not in the room for the related presentation by the committee on development (deve), commissioner de gucht has said he is very sorry to miss the discussion this evening as this is a communication he attaches particular importance to. those of you who are inta members will recall that, at the beginning of the commission’s mandate, some of you were unhappy with the relatively limited attention paid to trade and development in an earlier communication on trade, growth and world affairs. but the choice was deliberate. commissioner de gucht wishes to devote a standalone policy proposal just over a year later, starting from the premise that the eu has to adapt its trade instruments to contemporary global realities. we are more linked than ever before to countries that are far away or have much smaller economies. this interconnectedness requires a mix of ambition to keep global markets more open and sensitive to inclusiveness and sustainability concerns. the committee for international trade is in the front line every time the commission makes new trade proposals. we have worked hard together on the gsp reform and the ratification of a number of new-generation trade agreements – most of them with developing economies. members of the committee have seen for themselves how sustainability concerns were addressed. in many respects, we were able to give deserved prominence to human, social and environmental rights, thanks to the new powers acquired by parliament under the lisbon treaty with respect to trade policy. more work remains to be done before the european parliament elections. the commission’s priority this year with respect to developing countries will be to ensure that the 9th wto ministerial conference in december delivers tangible results for the benefit of the poorest members of the wto, in particular through a multilateral deal on trade facilitation. simplifying logistics within a country and at international borders is actually an affordable way of securing visible development gains. we sincerely hope that other wto members will share our ambition. we have focused for years on most of the mr president, it is undeniable that the banks have had a great deal of responsibility for the crisis we are experiencing. any measure which can help to prevent similar situations from recurring is therefore to be supported. europe needs strong banks that are accountable to the economy and the public, and it is not acceptable for taxpayers to come to the rescue of institutions that are in difficulty because of reckless operations. the simplest solution, in my view, would be a proposal i have been making for some time, namely a return to a clear and distinct separation between commercial and non-commercial banks, on the model of the glass-steagall act of 1933 in the united states. this formula worked without problems until the end of the 1990s and i do not think it is a mere coincidence that since its abolition international financial disagreements have multiplied. in any case, the proposals we are discussing today have at least one clear merit: the commission has finally put a limit on the compensation and bonuses for managers in this sector. i think it is immoral for the perpetrators of disasters to be rewarded with millions of euros. just a year ago, mr antonio vigni, who is now under investigation by the public prosecutor's office, left his post as general manager of banca monte dei paschi with a fortune of over five million euros. now we know the damage he did by putting one of europe's leading banks on the back burner. i believe that linking remuneration to results is a logical and necessary measure, which may even help to restore credibility, which is now severely compromised. mr president, the european network and information security agency, which was set up in 2004, has made a considerable contribution in recent years, but it needs to be improved to meet the new challenges of information technology. the field of network and information security is evolving at such a rapid pace that what is appropriate now may not be so in the near future. in addition to a more precise definition of the agency's field of action, it is therefore necessary to give it an organisational structure with the flexibility to keep up with the times.
in writing. − since its establishment in 2004, this agency has been doing its best to fill a huge gap. it is no small task to ensure network and information security across europe, including by assisting member states where necessary. the skills acquired by these technicians are increasingly indispensable, to the point of being able to enhance them, as the colleagues at itre suggest. in addition, the principle of subsidiarity requires us to start cooperating with counterparts in other major economies, given the transnational nature of the networks we monitor. i fully agree with the conclusions reached at the end of the informal trilogues, and even more so with the work done in parliament, and i congratulate the rapporteur. finally, i believe that the choice at this particular historical moment to confirm the seat of the agency in heraklion (canada) is a good sign of closeness to greece and of helping the local economy through the pipeline that will be created.
in writing. − the enisa agency, created in 2004, has been extended until september 2013. the proposal aims to extend the system for a further seven years, modernise and simplify it through a series of recommendations, including the strengthening of the computer emergency response teams (cert) and the appointment of a coordinating function to overcome the shortcomings of the system. given the importance of the tasks carried out by the agency - support for eu policy and legislation, voluntary public-private cooperation, cooperation with international organisations, etc. - i am voting in favour of the proposal.
in writing. the proposed regulation aims to strengthen and modernise the european network and information security agency (enisa) and establish a new mandate for a period of five years. the evaluation of the proposed mandate of enisa shall be the sole responsibility of the itre committee. i agree with the rapporteur that further consideration is needed on the duration of the agency's mandate (5 years) and on the time limit for its evaluation (3 years), and i therefore voted in favour of the proposal.
in writing. − the european network and information security agency must be enabled to contribute to network and information security as it has done so far. to do this, it is therefore necessary to promote a constant updating of the system: the commission will be able to coordinate the parties concerned more effectively and efficiently than is possible through mere cooperation between member states.
in writing. − the european network and information security agency was established in 2004 to improve the security of the european community's information and telecommunications networks. by cooperating with the commission and individual member states, enisa ensures increased security of information networks and assists the commission in the development of relevant community legislation. the agency has proved to be a valuable tool in preventing and addressing problems in the member states. the commission has proposed to extend the mandate of the agency. in addition, given the rapid and continuous evolution of this sector, it proposed updating the role of the commission so that it could play its role even more efficiently and effectively. i am in favour of the commission's proposal to extend the agency's mandate and strengthen its role within the eu: the work of enisa in the field of information security is certainly more effective than the mere cooperation of the policies of individual member states. in a context of continuous change, i believe that it is necessary to strengthen its role so that it is prepared to face the challenges of the future.
in writing. the european union agency for network and information security was established with the aim of ensuring a good level of security in electronic communications and the protection of the privacy of personal data. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. following an updated study of the agency's usefulness and functions, it was concluded that the agency had achieved its objectives since its establishment in 2004, but that some further guidance was needed to improve its work in the coming years. the proposal for a regulation on the next period of operation of the agency discusses the most appropriate location for the agency, which is currently located on the greek island of crete. it also provides for greater scrutiny of the work of the agency by parliament, the establishment of an executive board and minimum standards for the evaluation of the agency's performance. i therefore express a favourable opinion.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending council regulation (ec) no 812/2004 laying down measures relating to the incidental catching of cetaceans in fisheries and amending regulation (ec) no 88/98. whale populations have declined dramatically, while tens of thousands of whales die each year in union waters. regulation (ec) no 812/2004, which is seriously flawed, focuses mainly on the use of acoustic devices to deter incidental capture of cetaceans, although the latter face various threats such as habitat degradation, collisions with ships and underwater noise pollution. for these reasons, i hope that this proposal will contribute to the establishment of a general legislative framework for the protection of cetaceans similar to the marine mammal protection act in force in the united states.

in writing. − with regard to the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending council regulation (ec) no 812/2004 laying down measures relating to incidental catches of cetaceans in fisheries and amending regulation (ec) no 88/98, amendments have been made to the commission text which provide, in line with the obligations of the member states, for the commission to submit, by the end of 2015, a legislative proposal concerning a general legislative framework to ensure the effective protection of cetaceans from all threats. this proposal is part of a context in which whale populations are in serious danger and are therefore drastically declining due to underwater noise pollution and habitat degradation. it is therefore desirable to discourage their accidental capture by specific provisions providing for the use of hearing aids. at the same time, certain amendments are being made to the commission proposal, namely a stricter definition of the circumstances in which the commission itself is empowered to adopt delegated acts. i therefore express my favourable opinion.

in writing. - from 1989, when relations between the republic of mauritius and the european union began, until 2003, they were extended until an agreement on fisheries was reached. in this regard, a fisheries partnership agreement and a protocol were signed in 2012. a financial contribution is provided to the republic of mauritius in lieu of the possibility for european vessels to fish in its waters. in addition, european vessels will have to take on board a number of mauritian seamen. the agreement therefore protects the interests of both parties, and if one considers that fisheries are not the main contributor to gdp for the republic of mauritius, it certainly appears to be beneficial for the country itself. i therefore express a favourable opinion.

in writing. - each member of the european parliament shall, for the duration of each session of the european parliament, enjoy immunity both in the jurisdiction of his state and during parliamentary proceedings. in view of this, however, immunity shall not apply if the member is caught in the act of committing an offence or if his or her removal is requested for serious and well-founded reasons. the case involving mr martin is one of aggravated fraud under articles 146 and 147 (3) of the austrian penal code. he declared a third person as a parliamentary assistant, although this person had presumably never worked for him in connection with his parliamentary activity, and therefore fraudulently induced the european parliament's services to pay out emoluments and social security contributions to that person. in view of the request made by the vienna prosecutor's office, and the finding of probable reoffending, i express a favourable opinion.
