in writing. − we start from the assumption that the 2006 directive does not, in my view, sufficiently protect farms in relation to the problem at hand. the commission has drawn up a plan to protect businesses from misleading advertising, but the rapporteur, and with him parliament, is of the opinion that further measures are possible and should be taken. for example, the adoption of a blacklist of deceptive advertising practices and of companies convicted of having done so is an important first step towards greater clarity. i also think it is very useful for the national authorities to cooperate with banks and credit institutions, to introduce provisions on collective redress in national legislation and to consider extending the unfair commercial practices directive.
in writing. - deceptive marketing practices, which consist in the dissemination of false information, have become more and more widespread in recent times, to the point of taking on more and more varied forms and using more and more unfair methods. the european union's concern is justified not only because of the financial damage they cause, but also because they cause market failures and distortions of competition, and affect the ability of firms to make effective choices. this also has a knock-on effect on consumers, who consequently have to pay more for products and services. we therefore support mr de jong's report which aims to control such practices. since the protection of businesses against such deceptive practices differs from one member state to another (for example, currently only austria and belgium have introduced a specific ban on deceptive practices in their legislation), it is necessary to ensure that in all eu member states additional and significant measures are taken to prevent and inform, as well as new rules that can lead to specific legal actions. moreover, as this phenomenon is becoming increasingly international, new cooperation with third countries will also have to be launched.
in writing. - in europe there are many companies, and unfortunately a growing number, which 'offer' their commercial advertising services fraudulently, that is, by deceiving businesses, often smaller ones, who may have approached them believing they had potential benefits which instead turn out to be real scams. one of the most commonly used techniques is, for example, to require companies to update their data in order to create a database which is supposed to be free of charge, but which in fact takes the form of automatic and onerous subscription to a business yearbook for a specific and binding period of time. austria and belgium have already introduced measures to prevent these specific deceptive practices, and i hope that other countries will follow suit shortly. strong european cooperation is needed to prevent this phenomenon, which is now being tackled by real specialists in the field: the damage to businesses is considerable, because it affects micro-enterprises in particular, which cannot bear further economic burdens, especially if they are caused by illegal behaviour.
in writing. the alarm bells sounded by this spanish company, which is suspected of being fraudulent, are worrying: deceptive marketing practices can take many forms, starting with annuities, payment forms, protection of internet domain names or trademarks, and fraudulent proposals of 'business opportunities', 'work from home' or 'get rich quick'. there is an urgent need for a better exchange of information between member states, which is currently lacking. member states should establish or designate a national focal point where businesses and other victims of fraudulent practices can report and obtain information on judicial and extrajudicial remedies, and receive assistance and advice to prevent and address different types of fraud. each focal point should also have a database to record all types of deceptive marketing practices, with examples that are easy to understand. we therefore call on the commission today to ensure that the exchange of information between national databases is smoothly coordinated, for example by facilitating the establishment of an early warning system to identify new unfair practices, while taking account of budgetary constraints.
in writing. − misleading marketing practices has become an increasingly serious issue in europe, particularly in regard to misleading directory company schemes. it has been reported that such companies have been inviting businesses to complete or update their business name and contact details, seemingly for free, whereas in fact these business have unintentionally agreed to be listed in a business directory at a yearly charge of up to eur 1 000 or more. other reported frauds include payment forms disguised as an invoice for services already ordered when in fact they have not been, unauthorised offers to extend the protection of trademarks in foreign countries, etc. protection against and the mechanisms of law enforcement regarding misleading market practices differ among the member states which leads to major legal and operative uncertainties for businesses. therefore, i voted in favour of this proposal.
in writing. - the european parliament, in plenary session, voted this morning on a resolution by mr de jong on misleading advertising and marketing practices. the latter take many forms: the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's trade mark protection is not infringed by any of the other community trade marks. the economic damage of these practices is estimated to be in the billions of euros, money lost by european companies, mainly smes, which prefer to pay rather than react and report such practices. protecting the many businesses that are victims of trade fraud is therefore one of the union's key challenges. i am absolutely in favour of a resolution which, in my view, brings to light and denounces a phenomenon too often underestimated by local and national authorities, a phenomenon which in italy is of crucial importance, given the strong presence of smes in the italian production fabric.
in writing. - the set of measures to protect businesses from deceptive marketing practices and to ensure effective compliance currently in force in europe is rather fragmented. that is why i am convinced that a clear regulation by the european union is needed to improve this regulation. moreover, deceptive marketing practices are not a european phenomenon. this is why international cooperation is so important in combating this phenomenon, with appropriate specific measures, because deceptive marketing practices can take on various forms which are very dangerous for the economy of companies.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner malmström, ladies and gentlemen, today is an important day, the prelude to the vote in the house tomorrow morning on a very intensive, fruitful and decisive work, carried out as a whole by the special committee on organised crime, corruption and money laundering. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful organisms. i would like to thank all of you in advance, from the chairman of the committee to the coordinators, the shadow rapporteurs and the individual members of the crim committee, who have made a significant contribution to the drafting of a text which, in our view, will certainly serve as a constant stimulus to the member states, the commission and the council. actions and recommendations after 18 months of activity, hearings, thematic contributions, expert activity on a mandate given by parliament in march 2012. the worldwide dimension and costs of transnational crime require this effort, and require it with great sensitivity on the part of all member states. one trillion for money laundering, 120 billion for corruption, a cost to the mafia that is difficult to estimate, but ranges from 4 to 5 points of gdp for the european union alone. we have therefore tried, together with our colleagues, to draw up a list of priorities, of concrete actions that we would like to be able to take together, actions and recommendations, with a time horizon that we have set for the next legislature, because we want a lawful economy, we want honest entrepreneurs to be able to compete in the competitions of any member state, excluding companies convicted of mafia, corruption and money laundering, so that they do not participate in activities within the european common market in which there are public economic resources. we wanted the crime of participation in a mafia-like organisation to be banned, we are against banking secrecy, we want banking secrecy to be abolished, just as we do not want tax havens in europe because it is important in terms of money laundering. we would like to refine tools such as confiscation and seizure, which ensure the possibility of acquiring resources that have been illicitly acquired by criminal systems; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules are applied in a fair and transparent manner. all this in accordance with the principles of proportionality and subsidiarity. a strong contrast to the drug trade, the smuggling of arms and cigarettes and the traffickers of death. commissioner malmström was recently in lampedusa and was able to see how important it is that these criminal systems, based on human trafficking, can be punished with effective and deterrent measures. there are 69 amendments, which i think are too many, and i have already asked the groups to withdraw some of them, and there are roll-call votes and split votes. it's an important activity. we must give europe a new tool, which will see the victims of the mafia remembered every year, every year from 23 october 2014, the year after that approval which we believe is auspicious for a common challenge all together to criminal systems, transnational crime, the mafia, corruption and money laundering.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to start by thanking mr iacolino, the rapporteur, and all the members of the special committee on organised crime, corruption and money laundering (crim) for this very interesting report. i am grateful that i have had the possibility on a few occasions to join its meetings and participate in its discussions. the report puts many important issues related to the effective fight against organised crime high on the european agenda. let me highlight a few particularly important issues here. i am pleased that there are so many concrete recommendations concerning corruption and integrity. for the time being, however, the commission does not intend to propose new legislation on the definition of corruption or on the approximation of statutes of limitation for corruption offences or the protection of whistle-blowers. there are long-standing international standards at the united nations (uncac) and the council of europe which cover a wide range of aspects of corruption. these are in place. with a few exceptions, the problem is mainly related to the lack of implementation of anti-corruption legislation, rather than definitions. the commission’s anti-corruption report will therefore look at the end results and the efforts of anti-corruption efforts. it will refer to all forms of corruption in the public and private sectors, and it will assess member states’ efforts to see what has worked and what has not worked and recommend further improvements and disseminate good practices. we agree with your recommendations regarding the fight against money laundering. the recently proposed fourth anti-money laundering directive addresses several of your recommendations. the commission is preparing a possible proposal for a directive on the criminal law aspects of money laundering. i am also pleased to see that several recommendations of the report deal with the confiscation and recovery of the proceeds of crime. i am convinced that we need an effective confiscation scheme in all member states, and i hope that the on-going negotiation on the confiscation directive will soon be completed. once this is adopted, it has of course to be implemented promptly. the commission also welcomes the recommendations on cybercrime. awareness-raising at national level will be valuable. as far as images of child abuse are concerned, there is already an obligation for member states under the child sexual exploitation directive. as you know, a number of initiatives have been adopted or are under way at eu level. this provides for a strategic approach and contributes to coordinating the efforts of different players. we have the cybersecurity strategy, the setting up of the european cybercrime centre at europol, and the coordination of national policies and priorities through the policy cycle for organised and serious international crime and other types of cooperation with countries through the global alliance against child sexual abuse online, with over 50 countries all over the globe now as members. we also have the recent cyber attacks directive, which lays down common rules on the definition of the most typical cybercrime offences and their penalties, as recommended in your report. furthermore, we have proposed a directive on network security. so, you see, we have a very ambitious set of newly-adopted actions, though for the moment we are not committing, from the commission’s side, to propose an eu action plan on cybercrime. the commission also welcomes the very large number of recommendations addressing the issue of trafficking in human beings, and that reflects parliament’s very strong commitment as regards this horrible violation of human rights. we welcome the focus on the implementation of the eu legal and policy framework on trafficking in human beings, and particularly the directive. the deadline for transposition expired on 6 april 2013, and still almost ten countries have not transposed that directive. i hope members can join me in pushing those member states to do this as quickly as possible. the directive on victims’ rights means that all victims of crimes will now benefit from common minimum standards on their procedural rights, support and protection throughout criminal proceedings. we also submitted, as you know, a proposal on europol in march 2013. this aims to enhance the operational effectiveness and efficiency of europol, while also increasing accountability towards european citizens. the co-legislators have started to discuss this, and i am happy that there has been good progress in parliament and the council. i hope we can see real progress and an outcome before the parliamentary elections. we also welcome the support from the european parliament on the establishment of the european public prosecutor’s office. that would be a milestone in the process of improving the protection of the eu’s financial interests and protecting taxpayers’ money. finally, concerning the cross-cutting aspects of organised crime, you refer to the idea of revising the current legislative framework, including mafia-type organisations, and for stronger action, specific witness protection measures or tailor-made investigation tools. we are currently carrying out a study on the effectiveness of the tools that we use to fight against organised crime. this will be done by next year, and it will enable us to determine the most suitable measures to be adopted in the future. thank you very much, mr iacolino and all your collaborators, for this very valuable report, which i am sure will be of extreme assistance for parliament’s work and for our work in the future.
the final report we are voting on in plenary is the result of a year and a half of hard work and complex hearings by the crim committee, a committee whose creation the s&d group strongly wanted. i am personally satisfied with the result achieved, although i would like to stress that this is only the first step and that unfortunately we still have a long way to go to spread a culture of legality in europe and to assert the principle that the mafia is not just a local phenomenon but a global phenomenon and must be treated as such. in this report we have outlined a path forward and tools to be improved or introduced to make the fight against crime, corruption and money laundering more effective. we now expect the european commission - and i am addressing myself to commissioner malmström in particular - to take our suggestions and turn them into proposals quickly. we as the european parliament, and in particular the libe committee, will be monitoring the implementation and follow-up of this report. i also ask the european commission to publish as soon as possible the first report on corruption in europe, which the commission itself has mentioned several times. the s&d group deplores this delay because we need to know the extent and the spread of the phenomenon in the member states in order to be able to combat it more effectively. we hope that the commission will publish this report by the end of 2013. as regards the content of the report, as the s&d group's shadow rapporteur, i can only congratulate myself on the inclusion in the text of some important proposals which we strongly wanted and supported, such as the common definition of organised crime and corruption, the harmonisation of criminal law on money laundering, the abolition of banking secrecy, the recognition at european level of the crime of mafia-style association, transparency in public procurement and, in particular, the creation of a blacklist of companies involved in corruption and organised crime, the rapid establishment of the european public prosecutor, the possibility of reusing the assets confiscated from organised crime for social purposes, the request for ad hoc legislation for the protection of witnesses and victims of trafficking, the reliability of european parliament prosecutors or other persons convicted for organised crime, and the introduction of stringent environmental standards for the victims of organised crime, which should coincide with the establishment of the european day of remembrance for organised crime and the establishment of a european day of remembrance for victims of organized crime, and the introduction of this report. in conclusion, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr iacolino, and the shadow rapporteurs for their fruitful cooperation, as well as the officials and assistants of the crim committee. finally, i would once again ask the european commission to implement our proposals as soon as possible and not to throw away the long and country reports. i share the thrust of the resolution, including the emphasis on the importance of implementation for the success of the policy, the overriding principle of democracy, rule of law and and i encourage this house to strengthen relations with our partners’ parliaments. we are at an important – even critical – moment in the implementation of the enp. its success depends largely on the willingness and ability of each country to clearly define and assume the ownership of reforms. european union policies can support but not replace this process. we also have to recognise that partners’ ability to stick to their reform commitments can be compromised by external forces. let me specifically underline the impact the conflict in syria has on lebanon or jordan. in such – but instruments at the european union’s disposal to respond to the challenges in our neighbourhood. we – the european union institutions and our member states – have to stick to our side of the bargain. we have to deliver on political engagement, improved access to our market, better mobility for people and strong and consistent support for reforms. as regards the eastern partnership, achieving a significant package of deliverables at vilnius will create the right conditions to maintain dynamism in the next phase. the major challenges ahead will be, first, implementation of the new agreements, making the process of political association and economic integration irreversible and unlocking the full potential of relationships with the european union; and second, shaping our relations with all six partners on the basis of our values and principles. let me be clear that these decisions on association agreements are sovereign decisions of those countries. let me also be clear that they are not about passing sovereignty to brussels. on the contrary, they are about strengthening their sovereignty by empowering these countries and using the association agreement as a vehicle for introducing european values. many of our southern neighbours are at a crucial phase in their struggle for democracy. conflicts and fragile security situations are threatening achievements already made continue with the implementation of our offer of more intense people-to-people contacts, easier mobility and gradual economic integration. the focus should not be limited to supporting individual partners. regional dialogue and cooperation in the mediterranean region remains as important as ever. it is important for building trust and contributing to finding a solution to the region’s protracted conflicts, and it is important for building concrete projects and concrete solidarity among the people. this is why i am encouraged about the recent ministerial conference on the role of neighbours, it is key to building the area of peace and prosperity that will fulfil citizens’ aspirations for a dignified life.
the resolution which we have tabled together with mr saryusz-wolski is a balanced one and lays the foundations for joint work between the european parliament and the european commission, which we hope will be achieved in practice, and above all it seeks to indicate the areas in which the european neighbourhood policy can be innovated, overcoming the limitations and mistakes of the past. the need for a reversal of the trend is dictated by the facts and the major changes and problems affecting so many countries in both the eastern and, above all, the southern dimensions. we have chosen as the main lines of our neighbourhood policy to build and consolidate healthy democracies in order to pursue sustainable economic growth, to define and extend the sphere of rights and to manage cross-border links. these fundamental lines must be pursued with strength and determination at all times. this means a genuine commitment by governments to free and fair elections everywhere, freedom of association, expression and assembly, as well as a free press and media, a rule of law administered by an independent judiciary and the right to a fair trial and, finally, efforts to combat corruption. in essence, the need in many countries to achieve the goal of democratic reform. the commissioner, to achieve all this, we must strengthen the application of the principle of 'more progress, more aid' and promote it through competition and positive cooperation between the partner countries. it is also necessary to encourage citizens to promote the universal values on which the european union itself is founded. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use is a good one. finally, we must adopt a new policy on mobility, including a new visa policy, which will govern, on the one hand, regular immigration, thus also responding to the problems that europe is showing in its demographic trend, and, on the other hand, promote a type of circular mobility that will help many boys and girls to study and learn professionally in our countries and then return to their respective countries to contribute to the processes of development and modernisation. in short, we must launch a more effective european neighbourhood policy, which combines the eastern and southern dimensions, dialogue and cooperation.

in writing. − as the world's largest exporter of goods and services and the main trading partner for over 100 countries worldwide, the european union is a highly open market. as we know, the opening of the internal borders of the european union has created a wide range of benefits and opportunities. less well known is the fact that many international criminal organisations often succeed in exploiting the eu's openness to trade to increase their illicit trafficking. this is the case with so-called "drug precursors", that is, substances that are themselves legal but can be used to make drugs. in order to combat drug trafficking and related criminal activities, the union has provided for special controls on drug precursors when they are exported, imported or in transit. until now, medicinal products have always been excluded from the scope of this special legislation. however, many drugs are used to synthesise narcotic substances, thereby indirectly fuelling their production and trade. this is absolutely unacceptable. i therefore voted in favour of this motion for a resolution which seeks to subject drugs at risk of diversion to a special regulatory regime and to provide the union with a rapid and effective response capacity in this field.
in writing. the report deals with the issue of drug precursor trade between eu countries and third countries. drug precursors are legal substances used to manufacture narcotics, which are often also used for illicit purposes. i am voting in favour of the report because the amendment to the regulation is essential to adapt customs controls in order to prevent this criminal phenomenon; in addition, the monitoring of exports, imports and transit should be increased.
in writing. − drug precursors are legal substances, but if intercepted by crime and misused, they can be used to produce drugs. for this reason, at union level, a council regulation provides that drug precursors, as classified and listed in the annex to the regulation, are subject to more or less strict controls when imported, exported and in transit. it has recently been discovered that medicines containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine are sometimes used to synthesise methamphetamine. the fact that medicinal products are excluded from the scope of the regulation makes it difficult to intercept or seize shipments of such products. the commission has proposed to introduce special legislation for medicinal products based on ephedrine or pseudoephedrine. i agree with the rapporteur that a new category of substances should be created to simplify the procedure for extending controls to other medicinal products which could be used in the future as drug precursors. adjusting the regulation, by means of the ordinary legislative procedure, whenever a new drug is used as a drug precursor would, in fact, entail too long a time-frame and undermine the effectiveness of controls.
in writing. − drug precursors are chemicals that have a wide range of lawful uses, such as the synthesis of plastics, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, perfumes, detergents or flavourings. they are traded for legitimate purposes on regional and global markets, but some of them may be diverted from legitimate distribution channels and used instead for the illicit manufacture of drugs. although control of drug precursors is therefore an essential aspect of the fight against drugs, the many legitimate uses to which they are susceptible preclude the possibility of prohibiting their trade. a specific regulatory framework has been established, both at international and eu level, to monitor the legal trade in these substances and to identify suspicious transactions in order to prevent these substances from being used for illicit purposes. we're keeping a very high guard.
in writing. − recent legislation on trade in drug precursors between the eu and third countries is a step in the right direction to regulate the trafficking of sensitive chemicals and pharmaceuticals, which are often and willingly used to synthesise drugs in clandestine laboratories or often even within the walls of the home. stronger rules, with clear information on imported or exported products, their weight, chemical components and routes, are useful in controlling trade in precursors and can help law enforcement to distinguish between those who use these substances for medicinal purposes on a regular basis and those who use them to produce drugs. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the rules on the protection of the environment are respected. this is likely to be undermined by the growing differences between customs offices at the eu's borders, which do not always carry out the same checks and often allow illegal substances to enter the single market in order to clear large quantities of goods quickly. i therefore vote in favour of this text because it guarantees greater security, transparency and legality for citizens and companies in the pharmaceutical sector.
in writing. - i thought it appropriate to vote in favour of the commission proposal amending council regulation (ec) no 111/2005 laying down rules for the control of trade between the community and third countries in drug precursors. firstly, because this proposal aims to fill a legal vacuum in the regulation. i think it is necessary to include medicinal products in the definition of scheduled substances and to create a new category of substances, so that the controls applicable to scheduled substances are carried out in a slightly more flexible way. this is to avoid recourse to the codecision procedure, which does not have a rapid response capacity and allows drug traffickers to adapt to the situation even before the text is adopted. this would prevent us from achieving our objectives of combating drug trafficking and organised crime as we should.
in writing. − i fully support this report because it strengthens the control of trade in drug precursors, especially of acetic anhydride which is often used for the illicit production of heroin. it is very important to create an eu system of licensing and registration capable of monitoring the trade of substances which are widely used in various legitimate industrial processes, but which can also be misused by criminals. the harmonisation of licencing requirements across the eu is essential for the prevention of market fragmentation and illegal transactions. in addition i hope that effective eu action in this field will encourage other regions in the world to follow the eu’s example.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the hedh report on 'drug precursors' because i believe that strengthening the system of control and data collection on operators and purchasers of substances which could be used for the preparation of illegal drugs is a matter of fundamental importance.
in writing. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be given the right to vote on the proposals for directives on the protection of the environment and the protection of the health of workers. the commission's particular attention to solving a delicate dilemma, balancing the reasons for combating drug trafficking with the delicate aspects of freedom of enterprise and, more generally, fundamental rights as defined in the lisbon treaty, should be acknowledged. in particular, it is important not to impede normal economic activities, especially in the chemical sector, by encroaching on the sphere of the minute management of security and police measures. the fact that small amounts of precursors are sufficient to produce large quantities of drugs is not helpful and would put us at risk of intervening with destructive or ineffective measures. the commission was able to find a proportionate and appropriate solution by using the specific subcategory which also concerns the end-users of precursors. if the competent authorities can ensure that data is handled correctly, we can say that we have done what was reasonably possible from the point of view of regulatory reform. i therefore vote in favour.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report which supports the general line adopted by the commission to tackle the problem of the illicit diversion of drug precursors (i.e. substances which are themselves legal but which can be used to manufacture drugs). effective surveillance systems must be put in place to prevent these substances from being diverted from eu lawful trade to fuel drug trafficking. in this respect, the proposal to strengthen the rules on the registration of drug precursors and the establishment of a european database on these substances is a major improvement on the current situation, giving organized crime a foothold and thus weakening its chances of illegally establishing itself on the european market.
in writing. − the report focuses on data processing, which must be carried out in an anonymous form under the supervision of the european data protection supervisor. i am in favour of this because the aim is to increase controls and ensure privacy, so as to reduce the supply of illicit drugs prepared using drug precursors.
in writing. − the eu has recently been criticised internationally for the alleged weakness of control measures on the european market for drug precursors. these chemicals are used in many industrial processes, but their legitimate trade is diverted to the illicit production of narcotics. drug precursors are rarely produced by criminals, because their manufacture requires major infrastructure: they're usually stolen or bought legally. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of pesticides and the use of pesticides in the manufacture of foodstuffs. the establishment of a strengthened and harmonised licensing and registration system, the establishment of a european-wide database containing information on seizures of drug precursors in the eu and the establishment of a list of all authorised or registered operators and end-users of drug precursors in the eu. these instruments will allow trade flows to be monitored more closely without imposing unnecessary administrative burdens on firms.
in writing. - today we voted on two reports on drug precursors, which are chemicals widely used in various industrial processes, for example in the production of plastics, in the pharmaceutical industry or in the cosmetics industry, but which can be misused for the illicit production of drugs. it was absolutely right and necessary to act in this area, because european legislation was very lacking. the european commission's proposal to improve the current situation is based on three main principles: strengthening the monitoring of trade in these products, improving registration rules and establishing a european database on drug precursors. the other legislative text is intended to regulate trade in these substances between the european union and third countries: the commission has also rightly chosen to apply stricter measures in this area. these substances, used illicitly, are mainly used to produce highly dangerous drugs such as cocaine, amphetamines and even heroin, which now accounts for the highest proportion of drugrelated deaths in the eu. i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report, which is a very good report, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report.
in writing. − drug precursors used for industrial production can be used by criminals for the production of illegal drugs. in europe, there have been concerns regarding the control measures used in the monitoring of the trade in drug precursors, particularly acetic anhydride which is used for producing plastics, dyes, perfumes, etc. but can also be used for the production of heroin, amphetamine and cocaine. therefore, it is important to make sure chemicals that are major components of illegal drugs are not diverted from legal trade in eu. i voted in favour of this proposal because it sets up a legal framework to better tackle drug-trafficking and prevent market fragmentation relating to drug precursors.
in writing. - the report by mr hedh on drug precursors was voted on in plenary today. drug precursors are chemicals widely used in various industrial processes, but which can be misused for the illicit production of drugs. despite the existence of a licensing and registration system to control trade, the eu has been the subject of some international criticism due to its allegedly weak control measures. criticism has focused on acetic anhydride ('aa'), the main precursor drug to heroin. i agree with the rapporteur in supporting the commission's proposal that, in order to ensure that these precursors are not diverted from lawful trade in the eu, end users of ad should be registered with the competent authorities and that a database containing information on seizures of drug precursors in the eu should still be set up, while respecting and protecting personal data.
in writing. − on the misuse of drug precursors, i thought it appropriate to vote in favour of strengthening the definitions used and introducing more harmonised and flexible conditions/requirements for registration in order to adapt the different categories to the changing situation. i welcomed the commission's proposal to set up a new european database containing information on seizures of drug precursors in the eu, and a list of all authorised or registered operators and all end users of drug precursors in the eu. the simplification and harmonisation of registration and licensing requirements within the eu should be supported to avoid market fragmentation and to prevent criminals from targeting the 'weakest link' in the eu internal market. finally, the establishment of a european database should be welcomed as it will bring the necessary transparency and strengthen control of all drug precursors in the eu.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution which aims to make justice and the judicial system more transparent and accessible to citizens, by digitalising documents and introducing electronic justice tools. i believe that e-justice can make an important contribution to streamlining and speeding up judicial and administrative procedures and reducing their costs. one small step on a long road ahead. the european union has repeatedly condemned italy for its failure to guarantee the right to a reasonable trial period, a right enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union.
in writing. − the first european multiannual action plan on e-justice covered the period 2009-2013. in today's vote, parliament called on the commission to put forward a new plan for 2014-2020 to relaunch the union's e-justice action while streamlining the legislative work, projects and financial planning relating to e-justice. the e-justice is intended to be a tool to make the legal system more accessible to citizens and professionals alike. the potential to be exploited is many: e-justice systems can facilitate the mutual recognition of judicial and administrative decisions, help reduce the costs of judicial and administrative proceedings and increase awareness of eu civil justice instruments and cross-border proceedings. the development of e-learning tools for the judiciary would be interesting and should be further developed in the new plan.
in writing. − justice has become one of the biggest costs in the eu. in addition to the unseen social burden, there are significant economic losses. long process times and the resulting insecurity lead to a substantial reduction in gdp. in this context, the digital justice plan 2014/18 aims to promote greater efficiency of procedures by automating the exchange of information, the service of documents and the translation of certain procedural documents. the objectives are the reduction of red tape, particularly cross-border red tape, and the development of e-learning tools for the judiciary and staff. in the report by mr lehne and mr lópez aguilar, parliament calls for the digital justice sector to be considered as a priority in the european justice programme for the period 2014-2020. i fully share the underlying demands of the parliamentary initiative of my fellow rapporteurs and, by voting in favour, i wanted to express my support for the path being taken.
in writing. − e-justice is a tool to provide greater access to legal and judicial information and to judicial and administrative proceedings for both citizens and professionals. we believe that e-justice can play an important role in strengthening mutual trust and understanding and thus in supporting the mutual recognition of judicial and administrative decisions between states, which is a fundamental principle of the union's legal order. electronic justice systems by their nature tend to reduce the costs of judicial and administrative proceedings, in particular by automating the exchange of information, the service of documents and the translation of certain procedural documents. we believe that this is in the interest of the various stakeholders within the judicial system and, on the basis of cost-effectiveness considerations, we believe that the projects should continue.
in writing. − i believe that e-justice is a tool to enable greater access to legal and judicial information and to judicial and administrative proceedings, both for citizens and for professionals in the field. the use of electronic applications, electronic transmission of documents, videoconferencing and the interconnection of judicial and administrative registers should be increased in order to further reduce the costs of judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings. this instrument will lead to considerable simplification of bureaucracy, and for these reasons i gave my favourable opinion.

member of the commission. − madam president, it has been almost a year since the commission adopted its proposal for a new european union environmental action programme. we are now approaching the end of a very demand-driven process. this house, as well as the council, has repeatedly called on the commission to propose a successor to the sixth environmental action programme, which expired this year. since then, you have had several discussions in this house about what the programme should focus on and why it was needed. both the committees made their opinions known and the member states adopted no less than four sets of conclusions. meanwhile, the commission consulted a wide variety of stakeholders during the programme’s development. what struck me most was the broad consensus that prevailed throughout this process. from the beginning, there was wide agreement on the environmental challenges we face, their importance for the economy and the priorities that should guide our efforts to tackle them. the result is a programme entitled ‘living well, within the limits of our planet’. that is the title the commission proposed, and it has not changed. but thanks to the work of parliament and the council, the programme itself has improved in many ways. the political agreement reached in june sends a clear signal that the european union and its member states support a strong and smart environmental policy in europe as a key condition for healthy living and a competitive, resource-efficient and low-carbon economy. this is well captured in the vision for 2050 set out in the programme. the programme itself is a joint commitment of the union institutions and the member states to deliver the benefits of environmental action to people and businesses all over europe. tomorrow’s growth will depend on making resource efficiency, natural capital and low-carbon technologies a much more central part of our economic policy. our competitiveness depends on eliminating waste and cutting costs, and moving away from an economic model based on extraction, production, consumption and throwing away. our well-being depends on further measures to cut the considerable risks to the health of our citizens from increasing exposure to air pollution and toxic substances. finally, we simply cannot afford to continue letting our natural capital degrade further, at the risk of losing out on the valuable and often irreplaceable services that nature provides. investing in nature is investing in our future. evidence shows that nature repays us many times over. i am therefore encouraged to see that the outcome of the negotiations between parliament and the council sets out a number of important objectives and targets to be achieved by 2020, for instance that we have to step up our efforts to implement the european union biodiversity strategy. we also commit to discussing and agreeing on a strategy for a non-toxic environment and to addressing the combination effects of chemicals and safety concerns related to endocrine disruptors and nanomaterials. under the programme, member states should work towards integrating environmental considerations, including water protection and biodiversity conservation, into land-use planning decisions. it also stressed the need to address european union soil quality, including through a binding legal framework. the european parliament and the council agree on the need to define our climate and energy targets for 2030, taking into account the indicative milestones set out in the low-carbon economy roadmap to 2050. finally, the seventh eap provides an ambitious framework for taking our work forward on the rio+20 follow-up. we now need to start elaborating on the eu position for goals and targets for poverty eradication and sustainable development beyond 2015. implementation is a cornerstone and a supporting theme of the seventh eap. the main elements of the commission’s proposals to improve implementation were all endorsed, including the need to further develop inspection support capacities at eu level and find effective solutions to access to justice. we will work closely with the member states so that each of us faces up to our respective responsibilities to deliver the environmental outcomes agreed as part of this programme. the new environmental action programme provides the medium-term framework for eu institutions and member states to join forces and implement the vision that we have defined. only by working together at all levels will we be able to deliver the improvements in the environment, the economy and society that we need to continue living well, within the limits of the planet. i would like to close by thanking and congratulating the rapporteur, mr franco, the shadow rapporteurs and the committee on the environment, public health and food safety for all their work on and dedication to this file. i would also like to state once again how much i appreciate the fact that the irish presidency gave such high priority to this file.
the seventh environmental action programme sets out a set of possible long-term policies to tackle the major environmental challenges, which can only be addressed through coordinated implementation of sectoral environmental policies, as indicated in the agreement we will be voting on tomorrow. only then can we begin the transition to a low-carbon, resource-efficient society, while safeguarding the health and well-being of its citizens. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's climate and energy policy and will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's climate and energy policy. i personally believe that legislative action needs to be accelerated to establish the three binding 2030 targets as soon as possible, so as to give all actors time to adjust to meet the long-term targets. the fight against climate change must continue to be an integral part of european action, and so we must continue along the path we have been following for some years now, namely the global approach in which all sectors of the economy must contribute in the perspective of achieving the ambitious 2050 targets, which provide for a reduction in emissions of 80 to 95 per cent compared to 1990. only strong and concerted internal action will enable the eu to play a leading role in the fight against climate change in an international context and to push for binding action involving global partners.

to touch on some of the issues you have mentioned in your reactions. regarding energy and climate and the plans until 2030, the commission, as you know, is actively working on the proposal with the aim of its being presented by the end of this year. on endocrine disrupters, i would like to be clear, concerning the strategy, that it is the aim of the commission to finalise the new strategy for endocrine disrupters by the end of this year. the strategy will be accompanied by a review of the old strategy from 1999, and this will also constitute our response to the european parliament’s own-initiative report and its action plan for implementing the decisions concerning endocrine disrupters in the current programme which we are now discussing. concerning the criteria: yes, our original plan was firstly, to propose scientific criteria to identify endocrine disrupters in the form of a commission recommendation, and then in a second step, to implement the criteria in the various new pieces of legislation. but given the vigorous debate in the scientific community, and also the claims by industry of the potentially high impact of the criteria on the availability of plant protection products, we are now carrying out both steps simultaneously. as a consequence, the commission will present proposals for the introduction of criteria to identify endocrine disrupters for biocides and plant protection products rather later than foreseen. this does not, of course, mean that endocrine disrupters are not regulated in those regulations. fourthly, concerning the soil directive, i would like to be clear that in the refit communication the commission did not propose withdrawing the soil directive. it did propose considering its withdrawal, and in the same document we have committed ourselves to soil protection in the way in which we proposed. so the fact is that, on the one hand we had seven years when we could not agree in the council to support the directive, and on the other hand, in the very programme we are discussing today we have a very firm commitment to deal with the soil issue. so i think it is an ideal opportunity, on the basis of both these things, for us to start seriously and immediately discussing how we really want to protect soil in the future. i do not think that it would be proper for us to leave it for the next seven years on the table like a kind of a sleeping beauty, because it is not of any help to the soil if we keep it for ten or fifteen years more. but it is important that we agree among ourselves whether we mean seriously to do the things to which we have committed in the seventh environmental programme which we are discussing today. i would just remind the european parliament that you have consistently supported the european soil directive from the first moment when it was proposed by the commission. regarding the other, wider, issues which we are discussing as part of our core economic policy, i think it is really important to understand where the world today is going. we are all used to the figure that there will be nine billion of us in 2045 – maybe 2040 or 2050. what does nine billion mean? it means that in one generation there will be two billion more people on the planet, which is more than the total population was at the beginning of the previous century. that is over 260 000 per day, which means in nine days the population of my own country is born – in nine days! – and that of belgium in seven weeks. that is the world in which we are living. so if somebody thinks that when we are talking about those issues we are talking long-term issues, they are simply mistaken. this is here and now. and if somebody thinks that this is not a matter that concerns european competitiveness, they are terribly mistaken. europe is a densely-populated continent. we are locked into many resource-intensive industrial models, business models, financial models, structures of the economy. we are seeing rapid rises in the price of many resources. at the same time we are seeing the volatility of those prices increasing. already today, we see that those prices represent more than 40 % of our cost structure – compared to labour, which accounts for 18 % of the cost structure in german industry, for example. we are very much import-dependent when it comes to energy, and also rare earths: just take a periodic table and i will show you how much of that we import from various countries. taking all that into account, if we are really serious about keeping industry in europe, we have to focus on producing products using less energy, less water, fewer raw materials, and re-using and recycling them, which is basically what we are proposing in the programme which is in front of us. that is our competitiveness if we want to protect it. in the next year i will be focusing with all my energy precisely on the green economy and the question of how we can help re-make some of the potential which we still have in europe. so i will be dealing a lot with waste, proposing and reviewing the waste targets, aligning all those waste targets precisely with the policy which we are discussing today in the orientations of the seventh environmental action plan, talking there about targets and indicators which are necessary, and also addressing specifically food waste, plastic waste, building waste and, basically, trying to make that proposal. unfortunately it will not be discussed in the course of the current parliament, but i think it is something that we all very much need to send to the future. finally, mr gerbrandy, you said that it would be better to have a european action plan to guarantee well-being, and that this shows that there is another way. i think you put it very well. i would actually correct you in that last statement. it is not showing another way, it is actually the only way. but we do not yet understand that this is the only way. but the sooner we understand, the better it will be for us. finally, i would like sincerely to thank the rapporteur again. mr franco, you have done an excellent job.
